‘We left with heavy hearts’: Israel’s assault displaces thousands in Hebron Submitted by Fayha Shalash on Mon, 10/26/2026 - 12:17 Condemned as collective punishment, Israel’s assault forces hundreds of Palestinians families from their homes, leaving them without shelter, stability or a clear path to return A Palestinian homeowner looks on as Israeli forces demolish his house in Hebron, occupied West Bank, 23 October 2026 (Reuters/Mussa Qawasma) Off Less than two weeks before her wedding, Mayar Amrish sat with her family in the spacious courtyard of their home, making plans for the big day. The 23-year-old Palestinian was preparing for her future, but within hours, her family home would be reduced to rubble. Outside the house in Farsh al-Hawa, in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron, Israeli forces were launching a sweeping demolition and forced displacement campaign. The assault, condemned as collective punishment against Palestinians, followed a shooting on Friday in which two Palestinians killed two Israeli soldiers. Israel imposed a total lockdown on the city and launched a wide-ranging military assault involving home raids, arrests, demolitions and the forced displacement of thousands of people. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Amrish’s family were among the first to be targeted. Their offence was living close to the site of the shooting. When Israeli media reports began circulating on Friday that the army would target such homes, Amrish rushed to gather clothes and essential documents. “Something inside me told me they were coming to tear it down,” she told Middle East Eye. “Sure enough, we had barely gathered a few items of clothing when soldiers surrounded the house and ordered us to leave,” she recalled. Just days earlier, the family had breathed a sigh of relief after an Israeli court informed them that the demolition order against their home had been suspended. The house had faced the threat of demolition for years because it was built in Area C of the occupied West Bank, which remains under Israeli administrative and security control. Since building the house in 2021, the family had spent around 30,000 shekels ($9,600), in addition to substantial legal fees and fines, trying to prevent its demolition. 'My father worked incredibly hard to build our home so we could finally settle down in our own city' - Mayar Amrish, Hebron resident But their reprieve was short-lived. Israeli bulldozers arrived and razed the three-storey home to the ground. The seven-member family were given no chance to remove their furniture from the 600-square-metre property, which had cost around 2 million shekels ($645,000) to build. As the demolition unfolded, Amrish’s parents lost consciousness as they watched years of hard work disappear before their eyes. The family is now staying with Amrish’s uncle while searching for somewhere else to live. “This house was the fruit of 25 years spent living abroad in Saudi Arabia. My father worked incredibly hard to build it so we could finally settle down in our own city.” A city under siege Following Friday’s shooting, the Israeli army launched an operation dubbed “Roar of Judah”, saying it would carry out extensive searches, seize weapons, uncover what it described as “terrorist infrastructure” and interrogate dozens of people across Hebron. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Since then, Israeli forces have sealed off parts of the city, carrying out raids, searches and arrests while forcing more than 3,100 Palestinians to leave their homes. Israel’s defence minister said those displaced would not be allowed to return until what he called “Hamas infrastructure” in the city had been dismantled. According to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club, 47 Palestinians have been arrested in Hebron since the assault began, while hundreds more have been subjected to field interrogations. The Commission Against the Wall and Settlements said Israeli forces had demolished a building containing three apartments, targeted commercial premises and shops, including a tile and ceramics company and auto parts stores, and bulldozed or damaged around seven dunums (0.7 hectares) of land. Most of those forced from their homes have been residents of Deir Baha and al-Jalada, in western Hebron. Yousef al-Jabari, the city’s mayor, said 488 families had been forced to evacuate, affecting more than 3,100 people. They include over a thousand children, dozens of elderly people, pregnant and breastfeeding women, people with disabilities and those with chronic illnesses, according to the city’s Support and Relief Committee, established to manage the crisis. ‘We left with heavy hearts’ The committee said 198 families were staying with relatives, 19 had moved into rented accommodation, and 22 had found other housing arrangements. Another 177 families reported having nowhere safe to stay. Hamza Shabana, 33, lived with his wife and their two-year-old daughter in an eight-storey residential building in Ein Deir Baha. The building housed at least 160 people. At dawn on Saturday, the family were forced to flee under threat from Israeli soldiers. 'We are all living in fear of an unknown future' - Hamza Shabana, Hebron resident Shabana said troops had surrounded the building and used loudspeakers to order residents out, showing no consideration for the children and elderly people inside. “My wife, my daughter and I left without being able to take anything other than enough clothing for two days; we departed our home with heavy hearts,” he said. Soldiers were stationed along roads in the al-Jalada and Ein Deir Baha neighbourhoods, directing displaced residents where to go. KP Governor Kundi says Sohail Afridi, assembly speaker 'in safe hands' after house arrest. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi said on Sunday that Sohail Afridi and Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati were “in safe hands” after being placed under house arrest. Afridi, who has become non-functional as the KP chief minister, has not been seen since the Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in his province on Oct 11. After their whereabouts remained unknown that day, a federal minister confirmed the next day that he and some of his cabinet members were in preventative custody . However, with no further details officially confirmed, Afridi’s brother and Swati’s cousin have approached the Peshawar High Court separately to seek their relative’s recovery. Appearing on Geo News ’ TV programme ‘ Jirga ’ aired on Sunday night, the governor — who now runs the province — was asked about the whereabouts of Afridi, Kundi said he had been placed under house arrest and was “in safe hands — there is no need to worry”. He said that if there were cases against Afridi, action would be taken against him and he would be indicted. However, if there were no cases, he would be released. Asked why Afridi was not being released if there were no cases against him, Kundi replied he could provide an update tomorrow regarding the matter. The governor further said that Speaker Swati was also under house arrest and would also be freed if there were no charges against him. Responding to another question, Kundi accused the PTI member of committing “illegal and unconstitutional” acts in his role as the KP Assembly Speaker. Asked how many people were self-arrested and how many were “genuinely” arrested, Kundi said he did not have these numbers but that about 40 or 50 per cent of them were “under self-imposed arrest or self-concealment”. The governor also addressed the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, stressing that it had been the “absolute last option”. Regarding the potential duration of the emergency, he said, “We will see … after six months are complete, we will talk about what will and will not happen. “But in my opinion, maybe it will run longer,” he added, clarifying that this was a “personal opinion” and he could be wrong. He said that the basis for saying this was that the Centre and province needed to be “on the same page” in the fight against terrorism and “streamline” efforts against it, and was making plans accordingly, which he believed would take some time. Kundi also distanced himself and the state policy from purported remarks made by Malik Khan Marjan — a member of the newly formed Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) for 12 districts of KP — wherein he favoured dialogue with the Afghan Taliban. “I will definitely check on this, but our policy is very clear: for now, we will not be holding talks with Afghanistan,” he maintained. The governor condemned acts of terrorism carried out against Pakistan from Afghan soil and criticised Kabul for “allowing” India to use its soil against Pakistan while also asking for dialogue. “If there is terrorism from there … our army knows how to fix it,” he added. “There is no dialogue and no talks of any kind about this.” “I think this is his (Marjan’s) personal opinion, but it is not our policy,” Kundi said.

Govt moves to establish new ‘umbrella’ privatisation entity. • Proposed legislation aims to merge Public-Private Partnership Authority and Privatisation Commission • Seeks to provide immunity to incumbent, former chairmen, secretaries and other officials ISLAMABAD: The government has introduced a bill in the National Assembly, for the establishment of a Privatisation and Public-Private Part­nership Commission (PPPPC), by merging the existing Public-Private Partnership Authority (P3A) and Privatisation Commission, to prevent duplication of institutional functions and processes. The proposed law that seeks amendments to both legal instruments — the Privatisation Commission Ordinance 2000 and Public Private Partnership Authority Act 2017 — also provides legal and investigation immunity to the current and all former chairmen, secretaries, board members, officials and consultants from any act of omission or commission in good faith and in personal capacity and commits public funds to contest any such cases. The all-powerful commission will be led by the incumbent chairman Muhammad Ali and will comprise a majority of members from the private sector, including two women directors. It will collectively administer four public funds — privatisation fund, public contributory fund, viability gap fund and PPP project development funds — created through allocation in the federal budget, receipts from international lenders, income from investments or any other source. The government claims that the PC Ordinance dealt with privatisation of SOEs under the government policy while P3A Act governed a separate body. Both frameworks were concerned with mobilising private sector capital and expertise in relation to public assets, infrastructure and services and their administration through two separate institutions entailed duplication of institutional functions and processes. Therefore, the government’s pol­icy decision was needed for establishing a single institutional framework and mechanism for carrying out privatisation and public private partnership transactions in an efficient manner. For this, it seeks to reconstitute the Privatisation Commission as the Privatisation and Public-Private Partnership Commission, to repeal the Public Private Partnership Authority Act 2017 and dissolve the P3A. The bill provides for the reconstitution of the board with a majority of independent members, including members with public private partnership experience and at least two women, fixed terms of office and clear grounds for disqualification and removal. The bill also empowers the proposed reconstituted commission to conduct functions of advising on, appraising, structuring, facilitating and monitoring public private partnership projects and the establishment of the viability gap fund, the PPP project development facility, and the public contribution fund. The draft claims that it provides a comprehensive legal framework for public private partnerships, including the contractual framework for PPP agreements, a federal PPP pipeline, the approval process, the risk management unit and PPP transaction execution committees. It also empowers the commission to set up PPP nodes within government agencies, settlement of disputes and an alternative process for below-threshold projects. The proposed law enables the commission to utilise public contribution fund to meet any government obligations with respect to PPP projects, including land acquisition, site handover, right of way and any such other enabling actions as may be required in connection with the project. All these funds would be non-lapsable. The PPP agreement between the public and private parties shall be a public document and any interested person shall be entitled to obtain its copy subject to applicable laws, and the government or the commission or the government agency shall not be held liable for any claim of the private party for a risk which is not specified in the PPP agreement. All existing contracts signed by P3A would stand transferred to the new commission without any disadvantage to the private parties. The proposed law empowers the commission to require in writing from any government agency to submit a complete list of its existing, proposed and planned projects, including projects under consideration or development, whether or not identified as PPP projects within fifteen days. The agencies shall be obligated to comply with such a requirement with full accuracy and completeness. Where a government agency fails to comply with any such requirement, the PC chairman may refer the matter to the ministry or division concerned for compliance. There will be a committee to review potential PPP projects proposed for inclusion in the federal PPP pipeline and shall provide its recommendations, which shall be placed before the board for consideration and decision. All officers, consultants, advisers, auditors, employees and other staff of the P3A shall upon the dissolution of the P3A be retained by the commission for a period of six months or until the expiration of their respective contracts, whichever is earlier, on terms and conditions not less favourable than those applicable to them immediately before the dissolution. Pakistan’s food supply fails own dietary guidelines: FAO. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s food supply remains sharply misaligned with national dietary guidelines, with major shortages of vegetables, fruits, roots and tubers, and pulses, while cereals and sugar remain in excess of dietary requirements, according to a Food and Agricul­ture Organisation (FAO) policy brief. FAO’s new policy brief, “Food Supply for Healthy Diets in Pakistan,” says ensuring equitable access to diverse, nutritious, safe and affordable foods is a policy imperative, particularly as more than 60 per cent of Pakistanis cannot afford a healthy diet. The situation contributes to high rates of malnutrition, while diet-related noncommunicable diseases are rising alongside persistent unde­rnutrition, the report says. Pakistan adopted its food-based dietary guidelines in 2018, setting out evidence-based recommendations for the types and quantities of foods needed for healthy diets. But efforts to promote healthy eating cannot succeed unless nutritious foods are available and accessible, the brief says. The assessment compared Pakistan’s annual food supply with population-level requirements across 10 dietary guideline food groups from 2010 to 2023, identifying surpluses and gaps. Population growth is adding pressure. Pakistan’s population increased from 189.3 million in 2010 to 235.2m in 2023 and is projected to reach about 330m by 2050. Climate change and other challenges are expected to intensify demands on the agrifood system. The report identifies persistent shortages in several nutritious food groups, particularly vegetables, roots and tubers, fruits, and legumes and pulses. The estimated vegetable supply gap widened from 10.9m to 17.8m tonnes in 2010 to 13m to 21.6 m tonnes in 2023. For fruits, the gap increased from 1.9m to 10.3m tonnes to 3.9m to 14.3m tonnes over the same period. However, milk, milk products, meat and eggs showed improvement. Fats and oils moved from a small gap in 2010 into the estimated required range in subsequent years. To address the imbalance, FAO recommends coordinated fiscal and regulatory measures to realign agricultural production and trade priorities, improve food distribution, reduce post-harvest losses and food waste, and strengthen demand for healthy foods. The brief calls for updating Pakistan’s dietary guidelines to reflect nutrition, health and environmental priorities, along with nutrition education and behaviour-change efforts. It recommends evidence-based taxes on beverages and foods high in sugar, salt and unhealthy fats, and front-of-package nutrition labelling to help consumers make informed choices. It urges greater agricultural investment in vegetables, fruits, pulses, roots and tubers, with support for milk production in some regions. Other recommendations incl­ude incentives for food processors to meet quality standards and reduce salt, sugar and unhealthy fats. Published in Dawn, October 26th, 2026

Pakistan, Qatar explore new avenues for trade, investment cooperation. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and Qatar have reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral economic ties, exploring new avenues for trade and investment, and expanding cooperation across key sectors, including agriculture, food security, manufacturing, information technology, maritime transport and infrastructure. The commitment was expressed during the second meeting of the Pakistan-Qatar Joint Task Force (JTF) on Trade and Investment, co-chaired by Federal Minister for Commerce Jam Kamal Khan and Qatar’s Minister of State for Foreign Trade Affairs Dr Ahmad bin Mohammed Al-Sayed in Doha. The meeting reviewed progress in bilateral economic cooperation since the inaugural session in April 2026 and explored practical measures to enhance trade, facilitate investment and develop industrial partnerships between the two countries. According to a press release issued here on Sunday, representatives of relevant Pakistani ministries participated virtually, while the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC), which serves as the secretariat of the Joint Task Force, coordinated the proceedings from Pakistan. Doha’s investment sought in modern agriculture, grain storage facilities and advanced farming technologies GCC Free Trade Agreement During the discussions, Pakistan emphasised the importance of an early signing of the Pakistan-Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Free Trade Agreement, seeking Qatar’s continued support in completing the remaining formalities. The Pakistani side informed the meeting that it had completed its domestic approval process and forwarded the approved agreement text to the GCC Secretariat on Dec 31, 2025. The proposed agreement is expected to provide a framework for strengthening trade relations and expanding market access between Pakistan and GCC member states. Pakistan also raised the issue of restrictions on its bone-in meat exports to Qatar and called for an early resolution. It highlighted that a comprehensive technical dossier addressing animal health and food safety requirements had already been shared with the relevant Qatari authorities. Agriculture and food security featured prominently on the agenda, with Pakistan highlighting a proposed MoU between the Trading Corporation of Pakistan and Qatar’s Hassad Food for rice supply. The proposal has been submitted to the federal cabinet for approval. Pakistan invited Qatari investors to explore opportunities in modern agriculture, grain storage facilities, silos, cold storage, integrated cold-chain infrastructure and advanced farming technologies. Both sides also discussed sustainable food supply arrangements. Besides, the Pakistani delegation presented investment opportunities in the automobile sector, particularly electric vehicles under the country’s new EV policy framework. Joint manufacturing, technology transfer and industrial partnerships were identified as areas offering scope for closer collaboration. Pakistan also invited Qatari investment in IT and digital infrastructure, shipping and maritime transport. The proposed Karachi-Hyderabad Motorway was offered as a potential investment opportunity for Qatar. The Qatari side stressed the importance of enhanced cooperation in civil aviation and air traffic. Pakistan welcomed the proposal and said aviation-related matters would also be taken up by the Technical Working Group on Logistics and Communications. Investment Fund Pakistan further presented the concept of an Investment Fund, highlighting opportunities for Qatari participation in infrastructure, agriculture, industrial development, information technology and other priority sectors. To translate the discussions into practical outcomes, Pakistan called for the early operationalisation of 11 Technical Working Groups identified during the first Joint Task Force meeting. These groups cover logistics, aviation, advanced manufacturing, mining and minerals, agriculture, tourism, financial technology, healthcare, education, industrial development, information technology and startups. Both countries reaffirmed their commitment to sustained engagement and effective follow-up through the Joint Task Force framework. Published in Dawn, October 26th, 2026

Mother can’t be denied child’s custody over second marriage, rules PHC. PESHAWAR: Peshawar High Court has ruled that contracting a second marriage cannot be a conclusive ground to deprive a mother of the custody of her child. A single-member bench consisting of Justice Mohammad Naeem Anwar declared that in custody matters the court was required to undertake an objective assessment of the minor’s existing circumstances, emotional attachment, settled environment, educational needs and comparative suitability of the proposed custodial arrangements. “It is a settled principle of law that, in determining the question of custody, the court must be guided primarily by the welfare, wellbeing and overall betterment of the minor, which take precedence over all competing claims and considerations, including the preferential rights asserted by either parent,” the bench observed. While disposing of a revision petition of a resident of Kohat, the bench declined to grant him custody of his minor son, but allowed him visitation rights. The petitioner’s counsel contended that, following her second marriage, the respondent (minor’s mother) was no longer entitled to retain his custody. Bench declines custody to minor’s father, allows him visitation rights “This contention, however, cannot be accepted as an absolute proposition. The mere fact that a mother has contracted a second marriage does not, by itself, furnish a conclusive ground for depriving her of custody,” the bench ruled in its eight-page detailed order. “The ultimate object is not to vindicate the legal entitlement of one parent at the expense of the other, but to ensure an arrangement most conducive to the minor’s physical, emotional, psychological, moral and educational development,” the bench ruled. The petitioner and his former wife were blessed with a son, but owing to matrimonial discord, their marriage was dissolved in 2018 and they separated. The minor remained in the custody of his mother, who contracted a second marriage in 2024. Subsequently, the minor started residing with his maternal grandfather in Shakardara area of Kohat. The petitioner had instituted a custody petition before a family court, claiming that the minor’s welfare, particularly his education, health and overall upbringing, necessitated his custody being entrusted to him. The trial court on Oct 16, 2025, partially allowed the petition and granted custody of the minor to the petitioner, while preserving the visitation rights of the minor’s mother. Aggrieved thereby, the respondents including the minor’s mother preferred an appeal before the additional district judge, Kohat, who, through the impugned judgment on March 18, 2026, allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court, thereby dismissing the petitioner’s application for custody. The additional district judge had held the petitioner entitled to visitation rights, subject to prior intimation to the mother and visitation at a mutually agreed and convenient place. The bench ordered that the minor should continue in his existing custodial arrangement, subject to any subsequent order passed by the competent court in accordance with law and the minor’s welfare. “The petitioner’s entitlement to visitation is recognised and shall be implemented through a definite and workable schedule. Since the minor has never previously remained in the petitioner’s custody, visitation shall initially take place on the premises of family court in Lachi, Kohat district, under arrangements determined by the learned judge of family court,” the bench directed. “The initial meetings shall be structured to enable the father and son to establish familiarity and develop a relationship without disturbing the minor’s emotional security,” the bench maintained. It directed that the parties may, by mutual consent, propose an appropriate schedule for visitation, which may include meetings at regular intervals and during school vacations. The bench also explained the mechanism to be adopted by the family court and the parties in that regard. The bench observed that in the instant case, it was an admitted position that, since his birth, the minor had never remained in the petitioner’s custody, not even for a single day. “The petitioner, therefore, has not had the opportunity to develop a direct and sustained relationship with the minor through day-to-day care and upbringing,” it ruled. “The minor is now approximately nine to 10 years of age and has been residing within the maternal family environment. In these circumstances, an abrupt transfer of custody to the petitioner, without first establishing a meaningful relationship between father and son, would risk disturbing the minor’s emotional security and settled routine,” the bench observed. It pointed out that both the petitioner and minor’s mother had contracted second marriages and were living with their respective spouses. “The minor has already been admitted to school and is passing through an important stage of his formative years. Displacing him from his existing environment in favour of a parent with whom he has never lived would constitute a significant change in his circumstances, without sufficient justification demonstrated on the available record,” the court maintained. ‘No shake-up in PTI committee structure’. • Spox rejects reports about core committee being ‘sidelined’ • ‘Strengthening’ of parliamentary body suggested, but not decided, says Panjutha ISLAMABAD: Amid a deluge of reports suggesting a change in the party’s decision-making structure, the PTI on Sunday rejected the notion that its core committee had been ‘sidelined’, or its powers re-designated to another body. Sheikh Waqas Akram, the party’s central information secretary, said the core committee, the political com­mittee and the parliamentary party were separate forums, each with their own, distinct responsibilities. Organisational and political decisions fell within the remit of the core and political committees, while the parliamentary party dealt with legislative and parliamentary issues. He said the parliamentary party’s recommendations were given due consideration and could be referred to the relevant committees, adding that final authority over all decisions rested with PTI founder Imran Khan, who had delegated powers to the committees. PTI leader Naeem Haider Panjutha told Dawn that during a meeting, Bar­rister Ali Zafar had suggested stren­gthening the parliamentary committee, but it was just a recommendation and no such decision was made. “Imran Khan had entrusted the political committee with the authority to make decisions, while directing that the core committee should also be… taken into confidence before decisions were finalised. The core committee had a large membership, which made decision-making difficult. That was one of the reasons for forming the political committee — to facilitate decisions and reduce the chances of discussions being leaked,” he said. He said that there was also a proposal to include heads of the party’s organisational bodies in the political committee. “Subsequently, the mandate for the movement and negotiations was given to Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Raja Nasir Abbas, while Sohail Afridi was entrusted with the authority to lead the street movement. How can any change be made without Imran Khan’s approval?” he questioned. Furthermore, the PTI also rejected a statement attributed to PTI interim chief Barrister Gohar Ali Khan suggesting that the KP chief minister could have avoided detention by staying in Mardan but he travelled to Peshawar as part of a “pre-planned master plan”. Imran, Bushra’s ‘ordeal’ Meanwhile, in a separate statement, the party condemned the prolonged detention of its founder and his wife, the denial of their fundamental and constitutional rights, and the use of state machinery to intimidate political opponents. The party warned that continued disregard for constitutional safeguards, due process and the sanctity of private homes was setting an alarming precedent that could threaten rights and freedoms of all citizens. In a statement, Mr Akram claimed that Imran Khan had spent 1,177 days in detention at Adiala Jail, including 356 days in solitary confinement, while Bushra Bibi had remained behind bars for more than 911 days. He said that the prolonged detention of both, restrictions on their meetings with family members, lawyers and party leaders, and growing concerns about Mr Khan’s health and medical care required immediate attention. He demanded that Imran Khan and Bushra Bibi be granted all their legal, fundamental and constitutionally guaranteed rights, including regular meetings with family members, lawyers and the party leadership. He called for appropriate medical care under the supervision of Imran Khan’s personal physician and a comprehensive examination by qualified medical specialists. He also condemned the continued detention of Imran Khan’s sisters, despite the completion of their reported 30-day detention under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) law. He demanded their immediate release, along with that of detained PTI leaders, elected representatives and party workers, adding that preventive detention must not become an instrument for punishing political dissent or silencing opposition voices. Sharp rise in prices of smartphones burdens consumers in Karachi. • Average cost of mobile phone with 4GB RAM and 64GB storage has risen to around Rs40,000 compared to Rs22,000 a few months ago • Dealers say while govt taxes have not increased significantly, rising cost of chips is affecting rates of new handsets • Market survey shows lower, middle-income groups hit hardest • Consumers say abrupt price hike hampers connectivity in digital age KARACHI: A sharp rise in mobile phone prices in the city has made new smartphones almost unaffordable for a large number of consumers as all major mobile phone brands have increased prices by Rs15,000 to Rs30,000 per handset. The increase has hit particularly hard those who could previously afford “budget smartphones”. The budget smartphone can be described as a device with bare minimum features needed to function reliably for daily essentials, such as 4GB of RAM and 64GB of storage. While it used to cost around Rs20,000 until last year, it is now priced above Rs30,000, and, therefore, has gone out of reach for many. Consumers wonder why the prices have gone up so much. Some think it is because of the taxes imposed by the government while others say it is so because of the US-Iran war that has affected international trade and, with that, export of mobile phone components. For a vast majority, education, work, online transport services, banking, government services and communication with family members are linked to smartphones and, therefore, having a reliable phone is essential. Due to a steep hike in prices, a large number of buyers have no option but to buy used phones available on the market or kit phones, which are refurbished sets imported in bulk without retail packaging to avoid heavy customs duties. However, many believe that used or kit phones do not offer the same reliability which a new smartphone does. Shopkeepers said the unprecedented increase in mobile phone prices had not only made life more difficult for consumers, but had also severely affected their businesses. One shopkeeper said: “When a phone costing Rs20,000 rises to Rs30,000 or Rs35,000, many consumers can no longer afford it. Our sales have fallen drastically following the increase in prices.” Another shopkeeper said the market was currently facing uncertainty because of continued price fluctuations and a shortage of supply. The ‘reason’ behind price hike The Karachi Electronics Dealers Association president, Muhammad Rizwan Irfan, said that there had been no significant increase in taxes to affect the price so much. He said mobile phone prices had increased mainly due to the rising cost of chips. Similarly, Mian Abdul Rehman of the Pakistan Mobile Phone Manufacturers Association told Dawn that mobile phones were becoming increasingly expensive mainly because of the rising cost of RAM (random access memory) and ROM (read-only memory). He said demand for memory components had increased significantly with the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, including its use in AI systems and robotics and data centres. However, their production had not increased at the same pace as consumption. “AI companies are buying RAM and ROM at very high prices, which is driving up their cost,” he said. Mr Rehman said memory device prices had remained relatively stable before the rapid expansion of AI, but the situation had changed with the growing demand from AI-related industries. He said mobile phone manufacturers were finding it increasingly difficult to absorb the higher cost of memory components. “That’s why there has been such a significant increase in mobile phone prices,” he added. Consumers seek govt intervention Perturbed by the jacked-up prices, consumers Dawn spoke to are calling on the government to take measures to keep smartphones with basic specifications within the reach of ordinary citizens, arguing that access to digital services should not become limited to those who can afford increasingly expensive handsets. They said mobile phones are an essential part of everyday life rather than merely a means of communication or entertainment. A customer at Sareena Mobile Market in Buffer Zone said phones are a basic necessity in everyday life. “On the one hand, the government talks about a ‘Digital Pakistan’, but on the other, the price of the very device through which ordinary citizens access essential government and other digital services continues to rise,” he said, adding: “The government should take measures to keep the prices of basic smartphones affordable, so that people can access essential government apps and other digital services.” Another customer suggested that the government enter into an agreement with a mobile phone manufacturer to make basic smartphones available to consumers at affordable prices. A man, who had come to Saddar Mobile Market to buy a new phone for his daughter, who just started college, told Dawn that he realised after visiting the market that buying a new smartphone was out of his budget. “When I came to buy the phone in August, I found that the price of the model I wanted had risen from Rs22,000-Rs23,000 to around Rs30,000. When I asked the shopkeeper about the increase, he told me that there might be problems with imports, which had pushed up the mobile phone prices. “With my salary and the current inflation, I could not afford an additional Rs7,000 to Rs8,000 all at once, so I decided to wait until the following month and save some more money. But the price has increased further this month. Now I have only two options: either buy a used smartphone or a keypad mobile phone, because a new smartphone is now beyond my means,” he said. A woman at the same market said rising phone prices had forced her to spend money from her savings to buy a new smartphone. “It is my compulsion to purchase a mobile phone at an inflated price as I am a working woman and need a phone in good condition,” she said. Speaking to Dawn at North Karachi’s Abdullah Mobile Market near UP Mor, a young man said: “My mobile phone was snatched last night near KDA Chowrangi. I have come to the market to buy a phone, but even for Rs25,000-Rs30,000, I cannot find a decent handset on which essential everyday apps can run properly.” He said: “Previously, a reasonably good phone with 4GB RAM and 64GB storage could be bought for Rs20,000-Rs22,000, but shopkeepers are now quoting Rs35,000-Rs40,000 for phones with similar specifications. Under these circumstances, I may now have to settle for a lower-quality handset, start using a keypad phone that can only make calls and send SMS messages, or buy a used phone.” Published in Dawn, October 26th, 2026

Brazil's leftist President Lula wins fourth term in dramatic comeback. Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched a re-election victory , but his rival Flavio Bolsonaro refused to accept the loss and said he would seek to annul the vote. With Lula’s victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries — such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru — all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump. The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied projections to win an unprecedented fourth term. According to official results, he won 51.8 per cent of the votes to 48.2pc for Flavio Bolsonaro, with Lula pulling around 4.4 million more votes. The senator is the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail term for attempting a coup after his loss to Lula in the country’s last election in 2022. Sunday’s vote was marked by confusion after a Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours as some polling stations had already closed. The move came at the request of Lula who complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting. Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some regions due to heavy rains, but he described the decision as “unacceptable” and a “dirty trick”. “It is impossible to recognise the results. I am going to request the annulment of these elections,” he said, stone-faced, in a brief speech in Brasilia. No candidate who lost the first round has gone on to win the second in Brazil since 1989, the first direct election after the end of the country’s military dictatorship. “People went to vote because we managed to convince them that voting was very important for ensuring democracy in the country,” Lula said in his first comments after the win. Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula’s Workers’ Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate. Lula’s fight back After the first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies, declaring “Never Again Bolsonaro” and revamped their social media strategy. The abstention rate decreased from the first round, falling from 21pc to 19pc. Julio Canelo, 42, a lawyer celebrating in Rio de Janeiro hailed a victory for “the entire democratic spectrum.” “It was the result of the people mobilising, in the streets and online,” he told AFP . A fierce social media battle drew in Meta, parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, which Lula’s campaign accused of favouring his opponent with “algorithmic manipulation”. Meta denied this but acknowledged that some of Lula’s campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors. “We are going to have to regulate them,” Lula said of social media companies after his win. A bitter campaign marred by scandals and mudslinging laid bare the deep divisions that have plagued Brazil over the past decade. A country split in two Lula heads into a fourth term with almost half of the nation having rejected him, desperate for change. He rose from poverty to become president in 2003 and was re-elected in 2006. Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. The charges were annulled on procedural grounds. In his third term, Lula oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters felt gloomy about the high cost of living and crime. Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, pitched himself as more moderate and jovial than his father and managed to galvanise conservatives as well as less ideological voters wanting something new. “We’re in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat — buying meat is out of the question,” said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro. Already one of the world’s oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030. He is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right. Lula’s campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump ’s United States. “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard,” he said on Sunday. Lula received congratulations from Chile’s far-right president, Jose Antonio Kast, and Ecuador’s right-wing Daniel Noboa — both close Trump allies. President Asif Ali Zardari also congratulated Lula on his “historic re-election”. He “expressed confidence that the longstanding friendly relations between Pakistan and Brazil would continue to grow, with enhanced cooperation in trade, investment, agriculture and multilateral forums for the mutual benefit of both countries and their peoples”, a statement issued by the Presidency said.

Saim Ayub released from Pakistan tri-series squad to work on batting form, Sahibzada Farhan named replacement. Pakistan opener Saim Ayub has been released from the national squad for the remainder of the ongoing One-day International tri-series after requesting to return to domestic cricket to work on his batting form and regain confidence, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) said on Monday. The PCB said the decision was taken after Saim spoke to head coach Mike Hesson, with the team management and national selection committee agreeing to his request. “Respecting Saim’s decision and appreciating his honest assessment of his current form, the team management and national selection committee have mutually agreed to accept this request,” the board said in a press release. Right-handed opener Sahibzada Farhan has been named as Saim’s replacement for the remainder of the tournament. The decision comes after Saim endured a difficult run in the tri-series, including a six-run dismissal in Pakistan’s dramatic one-wicket victory over England at the Gaddafi Stadium on Sunday. His early departure was part of a top-order collapse that left Pakistan struggling before Shadab Khan’s unbeaten 113 and an unbroken last-wicket partnership with Haris Rauf secured the win. Concerns over Saim’s form had also been raised ahead of Sunday’s match, with Pakistan captain Shaheen Shah Afridi acknowledging the selection options available to the team amid inconsistent returns from the opening batters. The PCB statement did not specify how long Saim would spend playing domestic cricket or provide details of any future selection plans. The latest change follows the inclusion of left-handed batter Maaz Sadaqat in the squad a day earlier. Maaz was added as cover for players carrying minor niggles after left-arm wrist spinner Sufiyan Moqim was released from the squad, with the PCB citing the nature of the Lahore pitches. Sufiyan was asked to return to domestic cricket. Maaz, 21, had initially been left out of the tri-series squad. An occasional left-arm orthodox spinner, Maaz now remains part of the squad alongside Farhan for the remainder of the tri-series. Farhan, meanwhile, returns to the ODI set-up after being left out of Pakistan’s original squad for the tri-series. He had been named captain of the national T20I side for the series against Sri Lanka earlier this month and led Pakistan at the Asian Games. Pakistan have already qualified for the tri-series final after registering three consecutive victories. They will face Sri Lanka in the fifth match of the competition at the Gaddafi Stadium on Tuesday, with the final scheduled for Oct 31 at the same venue. The ongoing tri-series, featuring Pakistan, England and Sri Lanka, is part of the teams’ preparations for next year’s ODI World Cup. Pakistan’s remaining league fixture against Sri Lanka will provide the team an opportunity to assess its options before the final.

#Watch #Chaudhry #Solar #foryou: Hotwiring rural Punjab. Muhammad Nazam pulls his smartphone from his kurta pocket, opens the YouTube app and plays a tutorial. “It’s not that difficult, you know,” he says. “It’s just two wires: one is hot, and one is cold.” That’s how he installed solar panels a year ago for his tubewell in Qila Mian Singh, Punjab. His neighbour Salim Mehr, clarifies, “When it’s installed, then everyone gets the experience. Everyone knows which wire is which, which button to press, how much to run it on, how many units are showing up, how much electricity there is.” This is the part of Pakistan’s solar revolution that didn’t make it to international headlines. News feature after feature marvelled at an energy transition motivated less by climate worries and more by the state’s persistent inability to provide electricity people could rely on and afford. (China’s untrammelled ability to provide cheap imports was a decisive factor.) It made sense that rich city households were rigging up, but what was driving the wildfire uptake across the countryside where, according to thinktank Ember Energy , 73 per cent of panel owners are now located. A singular panel propped up by a table in a market in Muzaffargarh Turns out there are two unexpected mechanisms at work: the effect of seeing a Chaudary install it and the ease of figuring out how to do it. Muhammad Imran and Muhammad Rizwan, for example, living half a province away from each other, had identical experiences with their solar PV installation. They asked the shopkeeper how to do it, watched a couple of TikTok videos, and did it themselves within an hour. All Obaid Ullah needed was TikTok to set up his single panel at his kiryana or corner shop. “It’s not a problem,” he says. “It’s very easy.” The panel, which is propped up with a stick, now powers a small cooler at his store. Spending several months across the rural countryside in Punjab, Zainaab spotted solar panels propped up on bamboo sticks, lying down amidst wheatfields, and spoke to people who brought them there. Travel for this research involved eight districts split evenly between North and South Punjab. She interviewed thirty-four people, mostly rural residents, especially large-scale (landlords) and small-scale (tenant and self-owned) farmers. She also spoke with solar panel importers and distributors, members of the Ministry of Energy and the Prime Minister’s Solarisation Committee. The research confirmed many prior insights, including, most prominently, the breakdown in trust in the state’s ability to fix the electricity grid and the resulting death spiral from utility bills. But two other findings stand out: the demonstration effect of rich landlords installing solar on their land and the ease with which such panels can be installed using social media. Even though they are critically influencing the rural uptake of solar, both dimensions have been curiously underexplored. Landlords as brokers Most new technologies find their first wave of adopters in well-off urban dwellers. Those with high rates of education, mobility, and wealth have both the knowledge of new technologies and the financial bandwidth to adopt them. For Pakistan, this meant that solarisation’s initial home was in the DHAs and Bahria Towns of the country. The residential make-up of these housing societies includes a cross-section of Pakistan’s elite, a central faction of which is the traditional landlord. These are families that have historically owned large swathes of cultivated land, and their incomes primarily come from the rents they accrue from large-scale farming in these rural areas, where they employ labourers, rent land to tenants and still maintain kinship ties. As part of the elite, they were also participants in the first wave of early adopters; many of them bought solar PV systems for their residential properties in Lahore, Multan and other urban centers. Some of these installations were well before solar prices had fallen to the level they have now. Anees Khawaja, a textile business tycoon and landlord based in Multan, first installed a 22-kW system in 2010, when, “it was the costliest solar. As well as the most inefficient…[but] Every year when we grow into solar, we get a better option available. So, this is here to stay.” Muhammad Mujahid, CEO of Innovo Corporation (which distributes several major solar panel brands across Pakistan), also identified landlords as the “first movers” with a “herd behaviour” following. What sets these landlords apart from the rest of the affluent class is their spatial fluidity between rural and urban areas. Aided by improved roads and communication infrastructure in Punjab, their economic, social and political bases transcend the urban-rural divide. Mohsin Iqbal, owner of Sharifabad farm in Okara, maintains a permanent family residence in Lahore but regularly commutes to Sharifabad. This is common practice for landowning families who travel frequently to rural areas where they maintain kinship and patronage ties through baradari networks and agricultural holdings. After having adopted solar in their urban houses and finding it cost-effective, the natural next step was to ease the financial burden everywhere, including in their rural farms served by diesel-powered tubewells. This meant bringing the physical solar panel and accompanying technical know-how to farms and villages before it had even fully permeated through the various class strata in large cities. In this way, these landlords became the unexpected agents of technology diffusion in rural areas. Shahida and her children in Sharifabad Mohsin Iqbal followed the same trajectory. His son Abdullah convinced him to install solar panels in their house in Model Town, Lahore. The system slashed their bills in half, which prompted them to solarise Sharifabad’s infrastructure too. The Iqbals had always provided free housing to labourers on their farm. Now, this now comes with free electricity too, as all the rooms are solarized. This has led to an influx of families converging on the 2,100 acre farm. Shahida’s family is one of them. She moved from nearby Dipalpur to the Iqbal farm. She has never been more than an hour’s journey away from her village but does not see solar PV (photovoltaic) as an alien technology but a fundamental part of her understanding of life and work. Solar adoption by landlords had a powerful demonstration effect on surrounding poorer communities, who were now exposed to a purportedly transformative technology at the very moment they needed an off-ramp from grid and diesel-based electricity. This exposure came through the most trusted channel possible: a kinship network whose members had already seen the technology work and could vouch for its benefits firsthand. Both information and demonstration effects were thus in play. Farmers heard it was beneficial and saw the proof themselves. Solar distributors are well aware of this phenomenon. Farukh Gilani, a Lahore-based distributor, put it bluntly: “A ‘ shehri babu’ [city boss] can’t impress them [farmers]… they will not trust you. They will only trust the people in their locality, even if they are wrong, so if landlords do it, they do it; otherwise, no.” He was right. Every small-scale and tenant farmer interviewed had travelled somewhere to see the panels and check their efficacy before buying their own. Muntazar Mehdi from Kundal Khokhran explained: “Some people a bit far away had installed it too… I went there and saw it. They told me that it was a very good job… So, I saw it and came here and installed it too.” In the village of Moazam Makhdum, Khadam Hussain said, “I saw that everyone around me had installed it. All their bills were forgiven.” This process was witnessed firsthand during the interviews, when Mohsin Iqbal stepped away to explain how solar works to a spectating labourer who then said he was considering installing solar PV in his own home. Ghulam Fareed stands in front of his solar panels in the fields For a small minority of tenant farmers, their landlords simply gifted them solar panels. These are cases of ‘paternalistic adoption’ where richer residents financially support poorer kin and tenants purchase assets, which solar panels are now seen as. Ghulam Fareed, who rents five and a half acres of land in Muzaffargarh, said his landowners bought him eight solar panels six months ago. They showed up with the panels, lay them on the ground and said, “it’s for our ease. It will be for the water, they said,” and taught him how to connect them to his tubewell. The gift came with no strings attached as his rent has remained stagnant. He now sleeps in a straw shed beside the panels to guard them from thieves. Muzamil from Garhmor had a similar experience, stating, “No, we didn’t install it. The chaudary [landowner] installed it. It’s his land. He just saw the system and saw it works well…He installed it in his home too.” Husain Shayq, Washington Post’s Pakistan correspondent, did not find this pattern surprising. In his story on the solar-powered transformation of Dhaku, a village in East Punjab, he noted that many interviewees were donating panels to poorer neighbours, explaining how, “The important thing was that the landlords or comparatively well-off people were willing to help by giving small loans to other[s], whatever they can do… maybe it’s part of their customs, their traditions.“ When pressed further, donors such as Anees Khawaja and Mohsin Iqbal both insisted that this was simply the gracious thing to do. Landlords, it seems, have played an unexpectedly critical role in facilitating wider solar adoption in rural Punjab. Solar and social media As solar adoption gained pace, so, too, did solar’s social media presence. YouTube and TikTok are replete with thousands of videos that provide information on brands, determining the size of the system one may need, and, most significantly, step-by-step guides to connecting panels to existing wiring, setting up their elevated structures and maintaining their efficacy. These are all in local languages like Urdu and Punjabi, and receive millions of views. Distributors like Farukh Gilani and Malik Waheed, based in Multan, create some of this content as advertising for their distribution companies. An example is Kamal Solar House , a distributor based in Multan, which has 122,000 followers on TikTok and posts content explaining different solar options almost daily. However, the majority of this content comes from electricians who post installation and maintenance tutorials. Usman Jutt Technical is one of these electricians, who has posted multiple series of step-by-step videos teaching solar panel installation in Punjabi on TikTok. This channel has 201,800 followers, and its last three videos have a combined viewership of 10.5 million views. These creators are based all over the country. AJ Electric on YouTube posted a tutorial installing a 6kW solar system in Taxila which amassed 800,000 views. Moreover, a Pakistan-based channel called Solar Power Easy Tutorials Hindi Urdu has gained over 30 million views and 261,000 followers. There is thus a thriving community of creators who actively disseminate this information. Viewers of this content are diverse. The audience includes everyone from solar customers to rural electricians. “Every single electrician has become a solar installer,” said a major energy company’s CEO in an interview, essentially proposing that an entire class of technical experts has trained itself online. His proposal was validated by the interviewees too, almost all of whom (barring those who hadn’t installed it themselves) had employed local electricians to do it for them. Sabir Ali’s installation in Kundal Khokhran was done by “boys from the village” who had learnt how to do it online. Not only is there an abundance of local installers, but the democratization of solar has allowed consumers like Muhammad Nazam and Muhammad Rizwan to become installers themselves, further reducing the financial load of moving to solar. Muhammad Rizwan with his panel that powers the fan in his hairdressing shop These videos are instructive for another reason. Produced by local people in local languages, they breed a comfortable familiarity with a technology that might otherwise feel alien. Access to a smartphone and the internet has effectively collapsed the distance between a technical expert and a small-scale farmer based in Kundal Khokhran, Muzzafargarh or Layyah, helping solar spread at an exponential rate. Therefore, while a landlord makes the benefits of solar technology visible, social media is what makes it usable. In the absence of formal training programs or even a consistent roll-out model from the state, the supply chain for this technology has organized itself into a contained, self-sufficient institution that can effectively localise this frontier technology. Farmers first see a neighbour’s tubewell running on solar and learn to trust that it works. They can then go home, pull out a smartphone and learn how to reproduce it. The offline and online networks reinforce one another. Each new installation becomes both proof for the next potential adopter and another site from which technical knowledge can spread. Solar has been truly life changing for many in rural Pakistan. Several respondents interviewed for this research had gone hungry to save money for electricity bills. They now call solar “God’s blessing”. The widespread adoption of solar in rural areas offers many lessons, foremost among them the power of informal networks and social media. These have allowed communities to organise so efficiently that getting an advanced technology like solar PV from a factory in China to a two-acre farm in Punjab is now, simply, a game of two wires.
