India to evacuate thousands as Cyclone Arnab nears eastern coast. Two states along India’s eastern coast were preparing to evacuate thousands of people ahead of Cyclone ​Arnab, which is expected to make landfall ‌on Wednesday, as one of them said it would close schools in some districts for two days. Arnab, which formed over ​the Bay of Bengal before intensifying into ​a cyclonic storm, is expected to make landfall ⁠in Andhra Pradesh state by Wednesday morning, with gusts of ​as much as 140 kph (87 mph), India’s weather office ​said. The cyclone will probably intensify further, it added. The weather system is expected to bring heavy to extremely heavy rainfall to Andhra ​Pradesh’s northern and central coastal districts, and southern ​regions of neighbouring Odisha. Andhra Pradesh has called for boats at ‌sea ⁠to return ashore and ordered speedy restoration of power in case of disruptions. A senior Andhra Pradesh disaster management official told Reuters on Monday the state government had ​identified 570,000 people ​as vulnerable ⁠and evacuations would start on Monday evening. Odisha’s government announced the closure of schools and ​colleges in five districts for Tuesday and ​Wednesday, ⁠and said it was preparing to move residents of low-lying areas to cyclone shelters. The Bay of Bengal is one ⁠of ​the world’s major regions for ​tropical cyclones.

JI threatens march to Islamabad in mid-November if petroleum levy not abolished. Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) Emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Monday warned that the party would march to Islamabad in mid-November if Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif did not abolish the petroleum levy. The JI has been demanding for over two months that the Centre abolish levies, including Rs114 per litre on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel, as the total prices have skyrocketed due to conflicts in the Middle East since March. A day earlier, the party said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal and Special Assistant to PM Rana Sanaullah contacted JI Vice Emir Liaquat Baloch and it was decided that a meeting between the JI chief and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will be held within the “next two days”. Addressing a press conference on Monday, Rehman said that JI had been patient and acted responsibly, considering the state of international affairs. He added, “Now, the responsible thing to do is for us to be aggressive.” “If the prime minister does not provide relief or abolish the petroleum levy, if he doesn’t take any steps, then in mid-November we will, with full force, march to Islamabad.” He suggested that the government accept the issues and “handle” them beforehand by providing relief to the people of Pakistan. Rehman said his party remained prepared to march towards Islamabad and recalled that federal ministers had contacted the party repeatedly. “Liaquat Baloch Sahib has told them that nothing will come out of talks until something tangible is given,” he said. However, Rehman acknowledged that the government had assured JI of “doing working” on the issue and “decide what can be achieved in the meeting with the prime minister”. The JI chief reiterated that his party will continue to stand by the demand. “We have told them the levy has nothing do with petrol’s price,” he said. Rehman wondered what could “federal ministers possibly tell prime minister about the issue” considering that the party had already submitted its demands. “We have never said no to a meeting but I want to say this clearly to the government that we don’t want a meeting so we can make an event out of it,” he said. The JI leader also criticised the relief package announced by the government in September, claiming that it was brought about as a result of JI’s protests in 42 cities. The “relief scheme” was announced for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Under the scheme, those having two-wheeled and three-wheeled vehicles would get a relief of Rs100 per litre on a monthly quota of 20 litres, while those owning small vehicles of up to 800cc would get a relief of Rs100 per litre for a monthly quota of 30 litres. Rehman on Monday said that the scheme was not enough for those, claiming that it did not cover various other motorcyclists, car owners or public transport. He further said the package did not address soaring prices of groceries and goods due to rising diesel costs. “Large political parties don’t even talk about nation’s genuine issues,” he claimed, adding that only JI had highlighted the concerns. Last week, JI said it would hold talks with the government regarding its demand to abolish the petroleum levy and on further high-level contacts between them. According to the statement, despite the planned talks, JI’s Baloch reiterated his party’s call for countrywide protests. On Aug 16, the JI announced sit-ins in all the provincial capitals of Pakistan against the petroleum levy and had called for a nationwide strike on Sept 3. However, when the day arrived, the two sides agreed to form committees to recommend measures to reduce the levies. On Sept 20, the party launched a protest march towards Islamabad, warning that if the government failed to abolish the petroleum levy, the protest could turn into one to oust the government. On Sept 22, the JI emir said his party, whose convoy had reached Multan, was postponing its long march at the request of PM Shehbaz, who had assured the other side of a meeting to discuss the matters. However, in a press release issued last week, JI alleged that the government had made no further contact regarding the planned meeting between Rehman and PM Shehbaz.

Makkah defence pact officials to visit Tehran today: Iranian state media. Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye will travel to Tehran on Monday, according to an Iranian and a Saudi official. Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency quoted the deputy secretary of Iran’s top security body, Ali Bagheri Kani, as saying that the visit was part of efforts to implement the idea of endogenous security in West Asia. Kani also told state TV that among the visiting dignitaries would be Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and Pakistan’s Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baqaei, said during a media briefing that the meeting with officials from the three countries would cover “most pressing issues threatening our region”, which included Israel’s expansionist policies, developments in Palestine and Lebanon. He added that the topic of “top priority on the agenda would be consequences of the US-Israeli aggression against Iran and its ramifications for the entire region”. IRNA further quoted him as saying that this meeting could be a prelude to further steps towards shaping “endogenous security — an issue that we have been insisting on for decades”. “We emphasise that regional security will not be ensured except by relying on the … security considerations of the countries of the region,” he said, adding that events of the last two years, especially the past eight months, had shown that sustainable and reliable security would only be made possible by “building trust and cooperation among the countries in the region”. In Pakistan, the military’s media affairs wing confirmed that CDF Munir was visiting Tehran, but did not share any further details. Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly also confirmed the visit in a post on X, saying that the meetings would be held today. According to him, officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye — the three members of the Makkah Defence Alliance — would hold meetings with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and security chief Mohsen Rezaei. Krimly described the visit as “part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Defence Alliance members for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis, and promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions, in support of the mediation efforts carried out by Qatar and Pakistan”. “The visit underscore the pivotal role of Makkah Defence Alliance members in reinforcing regional security and stability, and working with all countries in the region to achieve that goal,” he added. The visit comes as attacks by Houthis have spiralled over recent weeks and rhetoric between Washington and Tehran has grown more heated. Monday’s planned talks would be the first high-level contact between Iran and all members of the Makkah Defence Alliance since Saudi Arabia was drawn deeper into the conflict. Under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed in August, an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. CDF Munir had visited Iran last week as well. During the visit, Iranian leaders had conveyed that the US must take the first steps to rebuild trust, and that the acceptance of Tehran’s seven-point proposal could provide a starting point for renewed negotiations. According to Iran’s ISNA news agency, Baqaei said during the media briefing that the suggestion for the meeting was made during CDF Munir’s visit to Tehran last week. Tehran reviewed the proposal “favourably … and it is scheduled to be held today”, he added. War has engulfed the Middle East since late February when the US and Israel launched a wave of surprise attacks on Iran, just as Washington and Tehran were in the middle of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme. An April ceasefire brought an end to the initial phase of intense bombardment but the two sides have continued to vie for control of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel. Iran claims control over the strait and regularly targets vessels that attempt to cross without its authorisation, while the United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports. Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June deal which laid out a pathway to a permanent settlement. The war has since spread across the region to include fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

What challenges await Brazil's Lula in his fourth term?. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will have to wrestle with a divided Brazil, an unfriendly Congress, feeble public finances and a Donald Trump-shaped menace during his unprecedented fourth term. Days before his 81st birthday, the former union leader won Sunday’s runoff with 51.7 per cent of the vote over 48.2pc for his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro. The narrow result confirms the political divide that has split Brazil for a decade and shows that Bolsonarism remains strong, despite its far-right leader’s 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup. Here are the main challenges awaiting Lula in his next mandate. Governability As in his current term, Lula will not have a majority in Congress. Legislative elections earlier this month bolstered the right, making Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party the leading force with 121 out of 513 deputies and 28 out of 81 senators. To get his proposals through, Lula will depend heavily on the so-called “Centrao,” a bloc of centre-right parties that usually backs whoever is in power in exchange for benefits. Brazil’s President and presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva gestures to supporters after winning the presidential runoff election in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 26, 2026. —AFP But negotiating with them is becoming increasingly difficult, according to political scientist Mayra Goulart of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. Lawmakers now decide the fate of an ever larger share of the federal budget, she told AFP , giving them “more independence from the executive.” Money Economically, “Brazil’s three big problems are the fiscal problem, the fiscal problem, and the fiscal problem,” economist Mauro Rochlin of the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) told AFP. The state spends more than it collects, public debt exceeds 80 percent of GDP, and Brazil’s central bank maintains one of the world’s highest interest rates to contain inflation. The situation “could very quickly turn into an economic crisis,” said Rochlin. Supporters make an “L” sign as people gather to watch Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers’ Party (PT) candidate for re-election, speak after his victory in the presidential runoff election, at Paulista Avenue, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 26, 2026. —Reuters Adjustment is inevitable but difficult since it involves “unpopular measures” and confronting “very powerful lobbies within Congress,” he said. The challenge is likely going to clash with Lula’s flagship welfare programs, which have lifted millions out of poverty, and which he expanded during the campaign to win voters —drawing fierce criticism from the opposition. Insecurity The election campaign was dominated by security concerns, with violence a huge worry for many Brazilians. Accused by the opposition of having a soft touch, Lula will be under pressure to show results, particularly by tackling criminal groups and militias that control territory in several cities. On the campaign trail, he said he would support lowering the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 for heinous crimes, while the political right wants to reduce it to 14 years. Trump Lula campaigned on a pledge to protect Brazilian sovereignty as concerns grow about the broadening interventions of the United States across Latin America. Trump slapped tariffs on Brazil last year in retaliation for legal proceedings against his ally Jair Bolsonaro, followed by another 25pc tariff on some products this year. Brazil’s President and presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva gestures to supporters after winning the presidential runoff election in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 26, 2026. —AFP Brazil’s president will have to manage relations with Washington without relaxing his anti-imperialist tone, all while the Trump administration increasingly asserts itself in the region. Right-wing leaders across Latin America have meanwhile aligned with Trump in a trend dubbed the “Orange Wave,” in reference to the US leader’s complexion. Although ideology “matters for symbolic encounters,” it is “not that relevant” in practice, according to Oliver Stuenkel, an international relations professor at the FGV. He points to Brazil-Argentina relations as an example. “Deep down, the substance of the relationship hasn’t changed that much” despite Argentine leader Javier Milei’s insults toward Lula, Stuenkel told AFP.

Netanyahu denies reports of clash with Israeli army chief over Iran-linked operation ahead of election. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday denied reports of a clash with Army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir over a proposed military operation that could trigger fighting with Iran ahead of Israel’s election . Channel 12 reported on Sunday that Zamir requested a detailed discussion and signed legal authorisation from political leaders before carrying out their instructions. The broadcaster did not disclose the nature of the operation. The report cited military concerns that the political leadership could exploit tensions with Iran for electoral gain before the Oct 27 parliamentary vote. A security official warned that the operation could rapidly escalate into a confrontation with Iran and lead to a miscalculation at a particularly sensitive time. Netanyahu denied any dispute with Zamir during an interview with Israel’s Channel 14 later on Sunday. “There is no confrontation,” he said. Political officials also rejected the claim that the Iranian issue was being used for electoral purposes, according to Channel 12 . In the same interview, Netanyahu said he had instructed the Mossad intelligence agency and the military to work toward toppling Iran’s government. Channel 12 did not establish whether the undisclosed operation was connected to those instructions. Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Monday that reports of a rift between Israel’s army and its civilian leaders over fresh action in the war with Iran were “entirely baseless”. “The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF (army) on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false,” Katz said on X, insisting there was “complete” coordination between the two. Katz stated “unequivocally that there was no intention on Israel’s part to initiate an attack on Iran before the elections”. Opposition leader Yair Lapid referenced the report in a post on X on Sunday, accusing Netanyahu of seeking to put off the vote. “Tonight it was published that he wants to set off an escalation and a confrontation with Iran, just to postpone the elections,” he said. “This man has lost his grip. We absolutely must send him home.” Netanyahu also claimed Iran had resumed its nuclear programme and portrayed the election as a matter of Israel’s survival. On Sunday, he posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv alongside a warning about Iran obtaining nuclear weapons. Opposition party leaders Gadi Eisenkot and Yair Golan accused him of spreading fear and panic before the vote.

Pakistan condemns Houthi attacks targeting Makkah, Madina as 'grave violation' of Saudi sovereignty. Pakistan on Monday condemned Houthi missile attacks targeting Saudi Arabia’s Makkah and Madina regions, terming them a “grave violation” of the kingdom’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. According to a statement issued by the Foreign Office (FO), these “reprehensible attacks constitute a grave violation of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and demonstrate a blatant disregard for the sanctity of Islam’s holiest sites and the safety of civilians”. Pakistan reiterated its “unwavering solidarity” with Saudi Arabia and its firm commitment to the Makkah Alliance , the FO said. It reaffirmed its steadfast support for the kingdom’s security, stability and defence, including the protection of the Two Holy Mosques against any external aggression or threat. Pakistan also commended the “vigilance and efficiency” of Saudi air defence forces in countering the attacks, it said. A day earlier, the Muslim World League also condemned Houthi attacks targeting Makkah and Madina. In a statement, the Makkah-based organisation said the attacks showed “disregard for the danger of frightening the feelings of more than two billion Muslims, and the violation of the values of our true religion, and the most basic principles of humanity”. The condemnations came after the Houthis said they had launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, prompting the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Yemen rebel group to announce that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles as clashes between the sides intensified. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline. He also said the group had targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missiles fired towards Yanbu and Taif. Saudi Civil Defence said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Makkah and Madina regions. It said fragments of intercepted missiles had fallen in Wadi al-Mughammas in Makkah, as well as in areas of Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. The Houthis subsequently denied targeting Makkah and Madina, saying their operations were directed at “Saudi oil facilities and military bases”. The renewed fighting has shattered a UN-brokered truce reached in 2022 that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital, Sanaa.

Broken record: A 'holocaust' in East Punjab, literacy rates and the Palestine question. Two weeks after independence, communal violence, particularly in East Punjab, dominated the headlines, with the Quaid-i-Azam having to make a fervent appeal for peace. In other major developments between Aug 25 and 31, 1947, Madar-i-Millat Ms Fatima Jinnah reiterated the need for women’s literacy, Pakistan opened its first embassy in Washington DC, while different solutions to the Palestine question were discussed in the United Nations. In the Aug 25 issue, the headline of the main story on page one quoted the Quaid urging his countrymen to “Preserve peace for [the] sake of Pakistan’.” “Those who think they can undo Pakistan are sadly mistaken,” Mr Jinnah observed. He was referring to communal violence in East Punjab. “I have been watching with increasing grief and concern the orgies of violence in the Eastern Punjab which have taken … a heavy toll on Muslim lives.” In fact, in the Aug 27 issue, the lead story, describing the situation as a “continued holocaust in the East Punjab,” said that the violence in that Indian state had resulted in over a quarter million refugees. “Ferozepur, Hoshiarpur, Jullundur, Gurdaspur, Ludhiana and Ambala are still hotbeds of massacre and other brutalities,” the report added grimly. The Quaid reminded his countrymen to be wary and prevent communal disturbances in Pakistan: “It is of the utmost importance that Pakistan should be kept absolutely free from disorder. …” Mr Jinnah had good reason to be worried, for in the weeks after independence, Lahore and other parts of Punjab had witnessed communal killings, while in the Aug 25 edition, a report mentioned that Sardar Abdur Rab Nishtar, the Communication Minister, had to be dispatched to Balochistan to quell disturbances there. Unlike the present, the violence at the time was of a religious nature. “The situation is absolutely normal”, Sardar Nishtar claimed after a visit to Quetta. “I toured the area that was burnt and also Hindu and Sikh areas. I also went to the refugee camps and inspected arrangements for their accommodation and rations. … I feel that now by the grace of God, the situation is absolutely normal. …” Women’s literacy drive Also in the Aug 25 edition, Ms Fatima Jinnah hinted at the launch of a literacy drive for women. “Education,” the Quaid’s sister said, “was the pre-requisite for the advancement of any nation … at the earliest opportunity a big drive will be launched to stamp out illiteracy from amongst the women of Pakistan. …” These were of course progressive, noble thoughts. Some estimates indicate female literacy was under 10 per cent in Pakistan at the time of Independence, while being virtually zero in rural parts of the country. It would be wrong to say no progress has been made, as today female literacy stands at around 54pc. But have we done enough? Unfortunately, successive rulers failed to replicate the zeal Pakistan’s founders had for spreading literacy, even though several ‘education emergencies’ have been declared. The results of officialdom’s neglect over the decades? At least 25-26 million children of school age remain out of school today, while tens of millions of adult Pakistanis cannot read or write. One wonders what the founders of this nation would make of these abysmal figures. Good morning America The relationship between Pakistan and the United States has been a tumultuous one, with the former once being considered Uncle Sam’s ‘most allied ally’ in this region, helping fight an American anti-Soviet ‘jihad’ in Afghanistan, and experiencing numerous other ups and downs. That relationship, as documented in Dawn ’s Aug 26 issue, in a sense formally began on Aug 25, 1947, when the Pakistan Embassy opened its temporary quarters in Washington DC. “The Pakistan Embassy opened for normal business at the temporary headquarters at the Choreham Hotel today with Charge d’Affaires, Mr M.O. Baig declaring: “We are truly operating.” Our man in DC was scouting for a permanent embassy site in “overcrowded Washington” while observing that “My country is beginning from scratch in its relations with foreign countries. Therefore, there are various basic agreements that will have to be negotiated. …” Of course, the Pakistani mission in DC would later move to other buildings, but this long, complicated relationship began from a temporary abode in a Washington hotel. Palestine solution The Palestine question has remained unresolved for nearly eight decades, and at the time of Pakistan’s birth — Israel had not yet come into existence and the British were in charge of Mandatory Palestine — several solutions were being debated in the UN. According to a report in the Aug 28 edition, several proposals were discussed at the UNO (as it was then known) Special Committee Meeting in Geneva. According to one plan, the federal solution would result in the creation of six “cantons” in Palestine, “three Jewish and three Arab, having a Central Government on lines similar to that of Switzerland.” The other idea was for semi-independent Jewish and Arab states. Of course, none of these ideas would come to fruition, and the following year (1948) would witness the acceleration of the Nakba and the creation of Israel. As for the people of Palestine, they still await justice, and the right to live as free human beings on their own land. With the advantage of hindsight, one has the opportunity to study the historical cycles in a nation’s life. Thanks to this newspaper’s unique, extensive archive of back issues, one can examine the major political, economic and social trends that have shaped Pakistan and the world over the last seven decades and counting. Cliched as it may sound, history repeats itself, and we — as a state and as a polity — largely refuse to learn from it. Through this platform, we will look back at the ‘big’ stories that made it to the front pages of Dawn, as well as significant developments tucked away in the inside pages, from the birth of Pakistan onwards, and try to put them in perspective. We will study the critical issues of the week, starting from Aug 14, 1947 and examine the major themes and issues that made it to the paper.

Pakistan rejects Afghan Taliban's claims of civilian casualties in counterterrorism operations. The Foreign Office (FO) on Monday rejected allegations made by the Afghan Taliban government regarding civilian casualties in Islamabad’s counterterrorism campaign in the neighbouring country, maintaining that Pakistan’s conduct always “reflected restraint” and the response was “proportionate to the level of threat”. The Afghan Taliban have repeatedly claimed civilian casualties in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan; Pakistani authorities have denied the accusations, holding that they target military and terrorist infrastructure. Recently, a spokesperson for the Afghan Ministry of Foreign Affairs claimed in an interview with CNN that 1,119 Afghan civilians were killed or injured in Pakistani military strikes in Afghanistan since late 2021, according to Afghan media. In a statement issued on Monday, the FO rejected the “baseless and unsubstantiated” allegations regarding civilian casualties attributed to Pakistan’s counterterrorism operations. “Disinformation and misleading narratives will neither obscure the threat posed by the terrorist networks operating from Afghan territory nor absolve the Afghan Taliban regime of its responsibility to prevent Afghan soil from being used to plan and launch attacks against Pakistan,” the FO said, adding that attacks emanating from Afghan soil had claimed more than 3,500 casualties in 2026. It further said that various relevant United Nations mechanisms had reported the situation as well, and the issue had been raised as a serious concern for the international community. The FO noted that the Afghan Taliban continued to “shelter with impunity a large number of terrorist organisations, including the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and their affiliates, which continue to pose a serious threat to the peace and stability of the region and beyond”. It said that thousands of Pakistani civilians had been martyred in terrorist attacks, which it said were “planned, financed, supported and carried out” from Afghan soil under the “watch, patronage and active facilitation” of the Afghan Taliban. “No responsible state can remain passive when its civilians and security forces are repeatedly targeted,” the statement read. It maintained that Pakistan’s actions in response to terrorist attacks had been undertaken in exercise of self-defence, according to the principles of necessity and as a last resort. The FO further stated that the actions were “directed only and exclusively against terrorists and their logistical support bases in Afghanistan”. The statement stressed that Pakistan’s response had been “proportionate to the level of threat” and adhered to the principles of “distinction and precaution”. “The scale and scope of the action reflected restraint, particularly in light of the severity and frequency of terrorist attacks faced by Pakistan. Pakistan rejects any insinuations otherwise,” it said. The FO called on the international community to hold the Afghan Taliban regime accountable for “failure to uphold obligations” under various international commitments. “Pakistan reserves the right to take all necessary measures in order to safeguard its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the safety and security of Pakistani nationals,” it said. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from Dec 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — the Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. Ties between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been strained in the past few years as Islamabad continues to voice its concern over cross-border terrorism. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. September witnessed another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. This was followed by drone incursions from across the border, which Islamabad said were shot down, and two further rounds of retaliatory airstrikes. Over the weekend, the information ministry rejected former United States envoy Zalmay Khalilzad’s “baseless and misleading allegations” that Pakistan was “arming Afghans to fight the Taliban”. It also rebutted the Afghan Taliban’s stance that it lacked the “capabilities” to fuel insecurity in other countries and criticised it for resorting to “diversionary allegations” instead of preventing the use of Afghanistan’s soil for terrorist attacks against Pakistan.

Encounter culture. Ten suspected criminals killed in Karachi police ‘encounters’ in two days should trouble anyone concerned about public safety and the rule of law. Seven died in separate incidents on Thursday and another three on Friday. In each case, police reported armed resistance, exchanges of fire, and the recovery of weapons.These accounts may be accurate, but cannot be accepted without scrutiny. Officers confronting armed criminals have every right to defend themselves and others. Karachi’s residents, long exposed to street crime and violent robberies, deserve protection. Yet the frequency of these so-called encounters raises questions about how operations are conducted and whether suspects are given an opportunity to surrender. Whether the police actions were legitimate or unlawful can only be established through credible investigations. There must be forensic examination of weapons, independent verification of police accounts, and proper documentation of injuries and evidence. Such scrutiny should be routine whenever police gunfire causes death, regardless of the victim’s alleged criminal history. Otherwise, the public must rely entirely on the version offered by those who pulled the trigger. The concern extends beyond Karachi. In Punjab, where the Crime Control Department faces allegations of staged encounters, the political response has exposed a dangerous willingness to equate police killings with justice. After a suspect in the killing of a teenage worker in Multan died in an alleged encounter , PML-N lawmaker Hina Parvez Butt celebrated it as “justice served immediately”. She deleted the post but defended her remarks as public sentiment. Anger over a child’s murder is understandable. But an elected representative ought to know that public outrage cannot substitute for a trial, and that a police killing is not a judicial verdict. Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari criticised the comments, though the issue is larger than one politician’s embarrassment. Governments must make clear that police performance will be judged by crimes prevented, offenders lawfully arrested, and cases successfully prosecuted, not bodies counted. Independent inquiries into disputed encounters should publish findings and establish responsibility if unlawful force is proved. Police officers need training, equipment and supervision that make arrest a realistic option where possible. A force that can shoot but cannot build a case offers little lasting security. The police are duty-bound to protect lives. They do not have a licence to kill. Published in Dawn, October 26th, 2026

Jordan arrests 3 in dawn raid over church attack. Jordanian security forces on Monday arrested three suspects over an attack on a church last week that killed nine people, with the trio wounded in a dawn raid and shootout, authorities said. The kingdom’s Public Security Directorate said the group were apprehended at an abandoned house where they had barricaded themselves inside and opened fire on security forces. One of the suspects was taken to hospital in critical condition, while the other two were stable, Jordan’s state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka reported. There were no casualties among security forces, it added. On Friday, gunmen stormed the compound of the Greek Orthodox St George’s Church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate during a funeral procession, authorities said. Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between two and three per cent of the population. “Specialised investigation and raid teams apprehended the three terrorists responsible for the cowardly terrorist attack,” Al-Mamlaka said on X on Monday. The Public Security Directorate said the three suspects had “refused to surrender and opened fire on the security forces”. ‘We will show them’ Jordan’s King Abdullah II said in a post on X that security forces “chased them to the very end”. “We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he wrote. Earlier, the king visited the injured victims of the church attack in hospital, dressed in military fatigues and carrying a pistol on his hip. “We will show them,” he vowed. Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al-Mamlaka on Monday that the attackers were all Jordanians and “had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack”. “There is no indication of any external contacts or collaboration with foreign parties,” he said. Government communications minister Mohammad al-Momani said “we stand ready and will strike with an iron fist, without mercy or leniency, against anyone who attempts to undermine Jordan’s security”. Under Jordanian law, murder is punishable by death by hanging. On Friday, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered a three-day period of national mourning for the victims of the church attack, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions. Eight of the nine victims were laid to rest on Sunday next to the church in a funeral that drew a huge crowd amid a large security presence, AFP images showed. The ninth person, Mohammed al-Qasous, will be buried on Monday, his family said. On Saturday, officials at the church were digging a mass grave that was set to become a memorial.

LHC disposes of petition seeking release of Imran's sisters after govt extends detention. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday disposed of a petition seeking the release of PTI founder Imran Khan’s three sisters after the Punjab government informed the court that their preventive detention had been extended for another 30 days. An assistant advocate general of Punjab told Justice Abher Gul Khan, who has been holding hearings on the petition, that the government had approved a further 30-day detention of Aleema Khan, Dr Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi on the recommendation of the Lahore deputy commissioner. The law officer also submitted a report on behalf of the home secretary and said the detention period had been extended on Oct 7. Imran’s sisters — Aleema, Noreen and Uzma — were detained by authorities in September, under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960, as the PTI geared up for a planned protest march towards Islamabad. Their detention was ordered for 30 days and expired on Oct 19 for Aleema and Oct 20 for Uzma and Noreen, the petitioner’s counsel had said at the previous hearing. Today, counsel Rana Mudassar Umar requested the court to order the recovery of the three women and their production before the court. However, Justice Khan observed that while the deputy commissioner had issued the detention notifications, but the petitioner had not made the official a respondent in the petition. The judge held that the court could not issue an order beyond the scope of the petition. The judge disposed of the petition in light of the home secretary’s report. Aleema’s son, Shahrez, had filed the petition alleging that the three sisters remained confined at Kot Lakhpat jail despite the end of their initial 30-day detention orders on Oct 19 for Aleema and 20 for Noreen and Uzma. The petition stated that the women were taken into custody in September under Section 3 of the MPO, 1960. Aleema was detained on Sept 20, while Uzma and Noreen were detained a day later. The petitioner argued that the continuous detention beyond the notified period was unlawful, that the sisters were not wanted in any criminal case and that preventive detention could not be used as a substitute for ordinary criminal law. It asked the court to order the sisters’ immediate release and that they be produced before the court.

Central bank raises policy rate by 50 basis points to 12pc. The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) on Monday raised the key policy rate by 50 basis points to 12 per cent, its first increase since April as inflation, fuelled by high energy costs due to the Gulf conflict, remained above target. In a statement, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) said it had decided to increase the policy rate, with a majority decision of nine out of ten members. It noted that the “intensification in the Middle East conflict and low prospects of its near-term resolution” were keeping global energy prices at persistently elevated levels. “While the impact of this global shock on the domestic economy has remained contained so far amidst proactive monetary policy adjustment and continued fiscal discipline, geopolitical developments have worsened the inflation outlook as compared to the earlier assessment,” it said. It went on to say that although the external account and growth outlook remained broadly unchanged, risks had also increased. “Considering these developments and the evolving risks, the MPC deemed today’s decision as necessary to keep inflation expectations anchored, contain second-round effects of the ongoing supply shock and bring inflation within the target range of 5-7pc. This will help preserve macroeconomic stability, which is necessary for sustainable economic growth,” it said. It said that forex reserves had remained stable at around $21bn, Pakistan had reached a staff-level agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and that real gross domestic product (GDP) growth had been revised at 3.7pc, almost unchanged from the initial estimate. It further said that the Federal Board of Revenue had exceeded its revenue collection target during the first quarter of the current fiscal year, major central banks had raised interest rates in the wake of rising inflationary pressures and the IMF had also revised its global inflation projections upwards. “While noting these developments and the increasing frequency of global supply shocks, the MPC emphasized the importance of increasing external and fiscal buffers to further strengthen the economy’s resilience. The committee also reiterated that continuing the prudent monetary and fiscal policy mix, alongside timely implementation of structural reforms, is essential for achieving higher and sustainable economic growth,” the statement said. Regarding inflation, which eased to 10.3pc in September from 11pc in Augus, the MPC said that the re-escalation in the Middle East conflict and domestic wheat supply frictions were two major factors keeping inflation at elevated levels It said that their expected continuation over the next few months had “worsened the inflation outlook”. It added that there was a risk that elevated food and energy inflation may further increase inflation expectations, which may seep into core inflation going forward. “In view of these developments and increasing risks to the inflation outlook, the committee assessed today’s decision as important to keep the real policy rate adequately positive on forward-looking basis. This is necessary to bring inflation within the target range over the medium term. The inflation outlook is subject to multiple risks, including geopolitical tensions, global commodity price volatility, unanticipated adjustments in energy tariffs, further uptick in wheat and allied product prices and adverse weather conditions,” it said. Regarding the external sector, the statement said that exports were recovering, adding that remittances had remained resilient and were projected to turn out higher than the earlier assessment. It said that the current account deficit in FY27 was assessed to remain within the earlier projected range of 0-1pc of GDP. “This, along with higher financial inflows, is expected to increase SBP’s FX reserves beyond the current level. This outlook, however, remains susceptible to multiple risks, including elevated global commodity prices, tightening international financial conditions, and supply constraints,” it said. As per the statement, the committee expected GDP growth to remain within previously projected ranges of 3.5pc to 4.5pc in FY27. However, it added that the outlook was susceptible to risks from escalation in the Middle East conflict and adverse climate events such as El Niño conditions. SBP governor cites inflationary outlook SBP Governor Jameel Ahmed also addressed a press conference to announce the decision and said there were many “underlying factors” behind the decision, especially the inflation outlook. He cited the US-Israel war on Iran and its impact on energy and oil prices, developments in the domestic market and the subsequent impact on inflation. He said that nine out of ten MPC members voted to raise the policy rate, while one member had a different view; they were of the opinion that it should be raised further. He said that consumer expectations and other forecasters’ views were taken into consideration, as well as other macro factors, especially the impact of global commodity and oil prices on the external account and the impact of remittances and export trends. Ahmed noted a deterioration in the current account since the last MPC meeting. However, he added: “The good thing is that its impact is still between zero and one per cent of GDP and it will stay between that.” He also shared that the central bank revised its outlook on remittances, from $44 billion to $45bn. On exports, the SBP governor said the trend was witnessing an improvement; however, it was not yet in line with the economy’s needs. He added that the bank estimated imports to be close to $71bn. He said it would take longer than planned for inflation to get within the target range and revised GDP growth to 3.7pc for the current fiscal year ending June 30, 2027. Meanwhile, Topline Securities said the central bank had raised the policy rate “in line with our expectations”. Previously, the policy rate was 11.5pc. The central bank had held the rate steady since raising it by 100 basis points in April in response to rising global energy prices and supply chain risks — its first increase in nearly three years. The SBP has cut the key rate by a cumulative 1,050 basis points since mid-2024 , from a record 22pc reached in June 2023, as inflation cooled sharply from multi-decade highs. Last week, the IMF called for Pakistan’s fiscal policy to go beyond achieving primary balance targets and protecting debt sustainability by reinforcing policy credibility, fostering economic recovery and creating space for public investment and social spending to support stronger long-term growth. Additional input from Reuters

Imaan, Hadi move SC against IHC order refusing to stay trial in security breach case. ISLAMABAD: Incarcerated human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, on Monday approached the Supreme Court to challenge the Islamabad High Court’s (IHC) Oct 19 order refusing to stay the trial before an anti-terrorism court (ATC) in the security breach case. The case pertains to the alleged disruption of the security route of an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. The couple, accused of removing barriers from the route, was indicted on October 7. On Oct 19, the IHC took up appeals filed by Imaan and Hadi against the Oct 10 ATC order that rejected their petitions challenging the framing of charges and the inclusion of terrorism-related provisions. While issuing notices, the IHC had said it would decide how to proceed once the parties’ responses were received. Subsequently, the couple, through senior counsel Faisal Siddiqui, filed separate near-identical petitions before the SC on Monday, challenging the IHC’s Oct 19 order. The plea argued that the trial court proceeded with unprecedented haste by recording the examination-in-chief of six prosecution witnesses on Oct 10 and 14, and accepting the prosecution’s request to shift the trial to jail. The decision to conduct the trial in jail had also been challenged before the IHC, with the petition pointing out that the trial court had appointed state counsel . The petitions alleged that the ongoing trial was nothing but persecution aimed at subverting the SC’s order suspending the petitioners’ 17-year sentences in the controversial social media post case and at preventing their eventual release through an allegedly frivolous and mala fide case that had mysteriously resurfaced. Imaan’s petition argued that the IHC had “erroneously refused to exercise its discretion to grant ad interim relief to stay the criminal trial, despite multiple factual and legal reasons warranting such relief and repeated requests”. It said it was settled law that ad interim relief could not be denied in the presence of a prima facie case and where the balance of convenience favoured the petitioner, as she would otherwise suffer irreparable loss. The petition pleaded that Imaan had a clear prima facie case because recording evidence in their absence violated Section 353 (evidence to be taken in presence of accused) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), as well as their due process and fair trial rights guaranteed under the law. It further argued that the balance of convenience favoured the petitioner because delaying the trial for some time would not prejudice the prosecution. The plea claimed that the petitioner would suffer irreparable loss given the alleged gross violations of due process and fair trial principles in the proceedings, adding that it was apparent that the trial was leading to her criminal conviction. The petitioner’s liberty was at stake because of the denial of ad interim relief, the petition contended, adding that the IHC’s order was without jurisdiction, illegal and liable to be set aside. It further pointed out that the trial court had never dispensed with the petitioner’s personal attendance during the recording of evidence and that no proceedings under Section 540-A (power to summon material witness or examine person present) of the CrPC had been initiated. The trial court’s order of Oct 10 recorded that counsel had left the rostrum and the accused had left the video link. The Oct 14 order also noted that the accused had again moved away from the camera while their counsel had left the rostrum during the examination-in-chief of witnesses. Despite this, the court proceeded to record the examination-in-chief of six prosecution witnesses on the two dates. The petitions emphasised that the absence of the petitioners and their counsel was forced as a protest and had been recorded as such, but did not amount to a waiver of the right to be present during the recording of evidence. IHC hears plea against jail trial, appointment of state counsel Meanwhile, the IHC heard arguments on a petition filed by Imaan and Hadi challenging their trial at Adiala jail and the appointment of a state counsel . A division bench comprising Justice Raja Inaam Ameen Minhas and Justice Shahrukh Arjumand continued the proceedings, with advocates Riasat Ali Azad and Zainab Janjua appearing for the petitioners. During the proceedings, Advocate Azad noted that the decision to conduct the trial inside the jail had been challenged before the IHC. He contended that the accused should have been heard before such an arrangement was approved. Justice Minhas questioned the legal basis of the challenge, asking who had the authority to decide the venue of a trial and whether an accused could dictate where the proceedings should take place. In response, Azad said the petitioners were being brought before what he described as a “jail court”, effectively a cage, where access to the proceedings was restricted. He argued that the summary for conducting the jail trial had been initiated by an Islamabad superintendent of police and subsequently approved by the chief commissioner. According to him, the police officer lacked the authority to initiate such a summary, which he maintained fell within the federal government’s domain. The judge questioned whether a summary concerning a jail trial would have to be placed before the cabinet and also asked about the legal concept of an open court. Azad said he had not been heard before the decision was taken, despite the need to hear the defence. He pointed out that journalists and members of the public were not permitted to attend the proceedings inside the jail. He further submitted that the defence had requested the trial judge to pass a formal judicial order regarding the arrangement, but the judge declined, telling the lawyers to challenge the matter before the high court. The lawyer also objected to the appointment of a state counsel during the jail trial. Justice Minhas observed that the defence lawyers’ vakalatnamas (powers of attorney authorising legal representation) were still on the court record. Advocate Janjua clarified that she had initially represented the accused but subsequently withdrew her vakalatnama , explaining that travelling to Adiala jail every day was incompatible with managing her legal practice. Azad added that travelling to and from the jail took around two hours each way. When the judge again asked whether his vakalatnama remained on record, Azad said the defence had effectively been sidelined. He alleged that when he sought a single adjournment, a state counsel was appointed and the cross-examination of prosecution witnesses was conducted in his absence. Questioning the urgency of the proceedings, Azad said the first information report (FIR) had remained concealed for two years and that the accused had been arrested in the case immediately after securing bail from the SC. He further contended that although the original charges were bailable, a terrorism-related charge had subsequently been added. The counsel requested the IHC to restrain the trial court from delivering its final verdict until the petition was decided. Justice Minhas observed that the accused could also be acquitted, asking the lawyer why he was seeking such an order. Advocate Azad reiterated the request that the trial court be restrained from announcing its final verdict. After hearing the arguments, Justice Minhas remarked that the court would examine the matter. The bench did not announce a final decision on the request during the proceedings.

Lucky Group, Qatar Energy consortium quits Port Qasim LNG terminal plan over 'policy changes'. ISLAMABAD: Energas, a consortium of the Lucky Group and Qatar Energy, has given up a multi-million-dollar plan to establish a liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal at Port Qasim, citing fundamental changes to Pakistan’s energy policy, requirements and longstanding unresolved policy and fiscal matters, it emerged on Friday. On the other hand, the Port Qasim Authority (PQA) has warned Energas of terminating its final letter of intent (LOI) unless an “unconditional acceptance” is received on or before Nov 30, 2026, along with an updated status of the project. This would also result in forfeiture of the $2 million initial concession fee, PQA said. Subsequently, Energas has approached the prime minister for the refund of $2m, absolving it of any contractual lapse and instead blaming the government and factors beyond its control for not moving ahead. Informed sources told Dawn that Qatar Energy had booked an LNG terminal and committed to supply additional LNG quantities at around 10.2pc of Brent — almost the same rate it contracted to Pakistan State Oil under a second-term contract — to ensure full utilisation of terminal capacity on its own. Qatar has been seeking pipeline capacity allocation for LNG transportation through the terminal it planned with local partners near Karachi, a level playing field for LNG marketing and a terminal, and exemption from third-party access (TPA) that requires certain terminal capacity for use by government entities. Ahead of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s August 2022 visit to Qatar , Pakistan approved changes to the LNG policy to remove restrictions on upcoming private sector LNG terminals to provide their part capacity to the government. These were officially conveyed to the Qatari counterpart by then-petroleum minister Musadik Malik for re-engaging on LNG sector cooperation, including speedy completion of the LNG terminal and another long-term contract for more gas supplies on top of two existing long-term contracts, in addition to LPG supplies. While the energy situation kept changing, the project could not move forward over the subsequent three years as Pakistan sought diversion of its existing contracted LNG cargoes even before this year’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the Feb 28 US-Israel attacks on Iran and suspension of Qatar’s LNG production. Quoting past correspondence, Energas’s chairman Muhammad Ali Tabba complained to PM Shehbaz that PQA was “demanding” Energas’s unconditional acceptance of the final LOI by Nov 30, 2026, failing which PQA will cancel the final LOI and forfeit the $2m initial concession fee paid by Energas. He said the Lucky Group Consortium had taken up a self-funded project in good faith and in response to Pakistan’s energy requirements prevailing at the relevant time, which had since materially changed. “Energas’s inability to proceed with the project is attributable to two critical factors: firstly, a fundamental change in national energy policy and requirements, resulting in a clear frustration of purpose; and secondly, the persistent and longstanding unresolved policy and fiscal matters with the government, PQA and other government bodies/authorities, which have continuously impeded the viability”, he noted. The Energas chairman contended that those issues remain unresolved to date, which could have led to a final investment decision (FID) by Qatar Energy and Pakistani partners. “The government had committed to resolving these matters following discussions with the State of Qatar. However, despite the passage of time, the aforesaid matters remain unresolved, thereby adversely affecting investor interest,” Tabba said. He added that the national energy requirements and the policy environment had materially evolved since the project was originally conceived and Energas had already approached PQA for the return/refund of the partial concession fee. Energas said Pakistan’s official Integrated Energy Study (IES) — Final Report of March 28, 2025 confirmed that no new LNG terminals were required over the next five years. According to Energas, this “unequivocal admission” on the part of the government materially alters the circumstances and context in which the Energas project was conceived and directly affects the necessity and economic rationale for the project, resulting in a clear frustration of purpose from an investor’s perspective. It recalled that at the time of issuance of the provisional LOI in May 2020, the LNG Policy 2011 provided LNG terminal operators with a five-year tax holiday commencing from the Commercial Operations Date, but the exemption was withdrawn in June 2021 for new terminals while existing terminal beneficiaries continued to avail the exemption. This was attributed to conditions imposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF); thus, the proposed LNG terminal became “redundant and infructuous”, Energas said. On the other hand, PQA said the $2m deposited by Energas was not an ordinary refundable advance but an initial/partial concession fee under Clause 2.6(i) of the Project Guidelines 2019 that provides that this amount may be forfeited if the developer fails to fulfil the required conditions within the prescribed time, unless the parties agree otherwise. Furthermore, paragraph 27 of the final LOI required LOI termination and forfeiture of $2m in the absence of unconditional acceptance within the deadline. Highlighting Energas’s reasons regarding pipeline capacity allocation, execution of Gas Transportation Agreements (GTAs) with gas companies, allocation of tie-in area, exemption under TPA Rules and the income-tax exemption issue, PQA asserted that Energas was responsible for these developers’ obligations. “Project Guidelines require the developer to undertake the necessary surveys, investigations, environmental studies, hydraulic studies, detailed design and other project-related studies, and to obtain the requisite governmental and regulatory approvals,” PQA pointed out. It added that it was also the developers’ responsibility to have financing, design, construction, relevant access, regulatory compliance and other project requirements.

Curbing Criminal Economies in the Amazon Basin mloukili Thu, 10/15/2026 - 14:05 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Commentary / Europe 15 October 2026 12 minutes Curbing Criminal Economies in the Amazon Basin Criminal groups have taken over swathes of the Amazon, fuelling violence and environmental destruction through illicit business. In this excerpt from the EU Watch List 2026 – Autumn Edition , Crisis Group shows how the EU and member states can curb these activities and ecological damage. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Download PDF Full Report Download Full Report Select your download language English Spanish Also available in Español Español English Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy European Union Amazon The Amazon, the world’s largest tropical rainforest, is vital for planetary wellbeing. But it is also the source of several commodities, often obtained and sold illegally, that are in high commercial demand. Expanding markets for gold, wood, beef, critical minerals, wildlife, soy and cocaine, among other licit and illicit goods, have resulted in widespread environmental harm, including deforestation and contamination of soil and waterways . The alarming result is that parts of the Amazon are now releasing more carbon into the atmosphere than they absorb, contributing to global warming. Meanwhile, the crime rings involved in supplying some of these items have tightened their grip on swathes of the Amazon , particularly its rivers and estuaries. The profits they reap allow them to challenge state authority and co-opt officials. They use lethal violence against Indigenous and other residents to consolidate their hold. Europe is a major destination for many of the Amazon’s illicit or illegally produced goods. It is also at the forefront of efforts to contain global climate change, a cause that depends for its success on preserving ecosystems such as the Amazon. Yet European governments have been hesitant to address the intersection of trafficking and organised crime in the Amazon, which makes the job of preserving the rainforest much harder. The EU and its member states should work closely with South American partners to improve security cooperation, harmonise legal norms around environmental crimes, back Indigenous community responses aimed at curtailing illicit businesses and support the creation of legal livelihoods in the Amazon. This set of initiatives could help weaken the criminal groups bringing violence to the Amazon and limit the environmental damage they cause. Aerial view taken during a Greenpeace flyover of illegal mining areas in Kayapo indigenous territory in Para state, Brazil, on 19 March, 2025. AFP / Pablo Porciuncula Organised Crime in the Jungle Over the last decade, criminal groups have extended their reach across the Amazon, both to exploit its natural riches and to use its rivers to carry goods to seaports for shipment to European and Asian buyers. Governments in the Amazon basin have taken action to stop these activities, seeking to curb both the environmental degradation they cause and the attendant violence, but shifting political priorities and lack of resources have meant that the effects of their campaigns have been uneven. Criminals take advantage of discrepancies among the various countries’ penal codes to avoid running afoul of regulations and facing prosecution. For instance, Brazil prohibits the commercial export of many wildlife species, while Guyana and Suriname permit it under a quota. As a result, traffickers can catch animals in Brazil, move them across one of the borders and ship them legally from Guyana and Suriname without needing to forge documents. Shifting Drug Routes Drug traffickers have long taken advantage of the Amazon’s vast expanses and weak state presence to cultivate and process coca crops and transport cocaine, which they then send across the Atlantic Ocean. Despite prohibition measures, South American production of the narcotic is at an all-time high, spurred by a boom in consumption in Europe. In response, Europe has continued to focus its law enforcement efforts on drug interdictions , largely as shipments approach the continent’s ports. The U.S., for its part, has turned to military firepower, launching a wave of attacks on alleged drug-carrying boats along routes across the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean, killing almost 240 suspected traffickers so far. Some reports claim that these U.S. strikes have pushed additional quantities of drugs onto Amazon routes, but more research is needed to verify such a shift. That said, evidence does show that drug markets in the rainforest are more robust than ever: in Brazil alone, there was a 574 per cent increase in cocaine seizures in the country’s nine Amazon basin states between 2019 and 2024. With the state’s reach limited in much of the Amazon, traffickers move cocaine from Bolivia, Colombia and Peru to ports in the Guianas and Brazil. Barcarena, where the Amazon empties into the Atlantic, is among the most important exit points. Source: Crisis Group research; OpenStreetMap / CRISIS GROUP The limited reach of the state in much of the Amazon means that traffickers face few obstacles in transporting cocaine, which is produced mostly in Bolivia, Colombia and Peru, to ports in the Guianas (as the north-eastern part of South America comprising French Guiana, Guyana and Suriname is known) and Brazil, from where they ship it to Europe, either directly or via West Africa . Barcarena, the Brazilian town where the Amazon river system empties into the Atlantic, is among the most important exit points. Cocaine leaves through the Vila do Conde container terminal concealed in legitimate cargo, usually without the exporter’s knowledge. Recent shipments have been found in açaí , quartz and soy meal consignments bound for Portugal, the Netherlands, France and Australia. Crisis Group has previously written about how criminal groups in the region collaborate, with each playing a role in transforming coca into cocaine, moving it through the Amazon and distributing it worldwide. These networks encompass Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho in Brazil; the National Liberation Army or ELN, Comandos de la Frontera and other FARC dissident groups in Colombia; and Los Lobos and Los Choneros in Ecuador. All these organisations have employed violence and payoffs to quash local resistance and rid themselves of state agents who get in the way of doing business. But, reflecting what is happening elsewhere in Latin America, competition among criminal groups in the Amazon is also becoming lethal. Along the Orinoco River and Río Negro, shared by Colombia and Venezuela, a long-time alliance between the ELN and FARC dissidents of the Segunda Marquetalia came to an end in August 2025 , triggering clashes in which the groups used landmines and drones. As rivals jostle for control of markets, violence is likely to get worse. The expansion of organised crime is particularly pernicious for young residents of areas where they operate. These groups often hire children and adolescents to help with logistical tasks, paying them in drugs rather than cash. The kids then sell the drugs, causing substance abuse to rise in riverine villages. Along the Amazon River in Colombia, for example, Indigenous Ticuna people report that drug sale points have cropped up in rural areas. With no harm reduction programs in place, elders worry about the future of their children and the long-term effects on their communities. Gold and Other Commodities Many drug trafficking organisations have diversified into illegal gold mining, as rising prices for the metal have made it lucrative , with sales often raking in more income for criminals than cocaine. Illicit gold extraction can destroy ecosystems, as miners raze forests and pollute rivers and their banks with mercury (used to separate bits of gold from sediment). Mining sites have also been linked to grave human rights abuses, including violence against Indigenous leaders, sexual exploitation and child labour. Besides being highly profitable, gold is appealing because the product itself is easily transported and difficult to trace to its source. Even if illegally extracted, it can be funnelled into the legal supply chain at little risk just by forging paperwork. Criminal organisations seize this opportunity to “clean” drug trafficking proceeds by either investing in illegal gold mining or purchasing gold directly. The Guianas are a hub for these practices, as local regulations allow miners to absorb gold extracted in Venezuela and then re-export it as if it was locally produced. Over the past decade, much of Venezuela’s illicit gold has reached Switzerland and Belgium in this way , with large quantities also transiting Amsterdam. Security forces throughout the Amazon region are also concerned about Venezuela’s growing role in laundering illegal gold from Brazil and Colombia. After Caracas adopted a new mining law and U.S. sanctions authorities provided a licence for sales from the state company Minerven, illicit gold sellers have sought to mix their products into this newly legal pipeline for international sales. Law enforcement officials have told Crisis Group that “dirty gold” from other Amazon countries often passes through European airports for sale to refiners and minerals traders in countries including Germany and Italy. As with drug trafficking, competition over mines frequently results in violence. As with drug trafficking, competition over mines frequently results in violence. The ELN-Segunda Marquetalia fighting, which has spread from Venezuela into Colombia, was sparked by contests over gold and critical mineral mining sites as well as narcotics. In April, for example, these two groups battled in the Venezuelan municipality of Cedeño, displacing dozens of families . Other coveted minerals can also be found in the Amazon, including coltan, tin and tungsten. More than half the world’s critical mineral deposits are located on or in proximity to Indigenous lands. In Brazil, for instance, companies have sought permission to look for critical minerals in or near almost 44 per cent of the country’s Indigenous territories. The people residing in remote areas of the rainforest are often the victims of violence and other abuses committed by armed groups undertaking exploration. In Venezuela’s Amazonas and Bolívar states, coltan, tin and tungsten are mined in Indigenous lands that are under guerrilla control ; residents told Crisis Group that child labour, sexual violence and summary executions are frequent. To make matters worse, Venezuelan state forces in the area are reportedly collecting kickbacks from the groups, rather than protecting the vulnerable, and at times enriching themselves by taking more direct control of mines. Meanwhile, cattle ranching, land grabbing and industrial agriculture, the main drivers of Amazon deforestation, continue to grow as criminal groups launder money by investing in land, livestock and agribusiness. In Brazil, the expansion of agriculture and cattle ranching accounted for 99 per cent of native vegetation loss in 2025. What is at Stake for the EU Europe is tied to the violence and environmental damage done by resource extraction and trafficking in the Amazon because it is a major customer for the commodities in question. At the same time, the EU presents itself as a partner in forest protection and sustainable development as ways to mitigate the effects of climate change. But the attention paid by European leaders to the Amazon crisis has been fitful, due partly to sheer distance and partly to preoccupation with more immediate problems like the Ukraine and Middle East wars. European governments are also inclined to avoid engaging with Latin America in ways that might upset the U.S., particularly under the Trump administration, which has made clear it wants Washington to be the dominant influence in the Western Hemisphere. Even in law enforcement cooperation, which Washington seems to favour, Europe is keen to avoid any initiatives resembling U.S. backing for lethal armed force. The health of the rainforest and its inhabitants, however, is crucial for the EU in several ways. In recognition of its importance to achieving Europe’s climate goals, the EU-funded Amazonia+ program currently supports eight Amazon countries in tackling deforestation, forest degradation and wildfires. Germany and France, meanwhile, have pledged up to 1.5 billion euros combined to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF), a new Brazilian-led fund that pays countries for each hectare of forest they preserve. Furthermore, in March the EU adopted a binding 2040 target of slashing net emissions by 90 per cent from 1990 levels. While at least 85 per cent of that cut must be achieved domestically, up to 5 per cent of the remainder may be met by buying carbon credits from projects outside the EU (each credit will represent one tonne of emissions cut, or carbon removed somewhere else on Europe’s behalf). Cooperating with states and civil society in the Amazon could help meet these objectives. Another issue of acute concern for Europe is critical minerals. The EU and its member states are keen to diversify imports of these minerals , which have important applications in the green, digital, defence and aerospace sectors, and the Amazon is well positioned to form part of its supply chains. At present, Europe relies heavily on China, which builds more than 90 per cent of the world’s rare earth magnets and dominates refining of these elements. The EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act aims to ensure EU access to a secure and sustainable supply of these materials. Of the 34 minerals on the EU’s critical raw materials list , 25 are extracted in Latin America. Brussels has already established partnerships with two Latin American countries, Argentina and Chile , aimed at boosting cooperation on critical raw mineral extraction, while negotiations with Brazil are under way. Brazil already supplies over 80 per cent of the EU’s niobium, with most of its unprocessed copper coming from Brazil, Peru and Chile. Responsible mining investment in Latin America could help European countries acquire these valuable elements while limiting the harmful consequences for local communities and the environment. The EU has already adopted rules to address concerns about criminal profiteering and abuses in the mineral supply chain. But these are restricted in scope, and some have yet to kick in. The EU’s Conflict Minerals Regulation requires importers to carry out due diligence to guarantee their supply chains are not funding armed groups, violence or abuses, though it applies only to tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold, not the full list of critical raw materials. Another initiative, the Critical Raw Materials Act , allows the EU to fast-track certain projects, so long as they put environmental, social and human rights safeguards in place. Yet only a small subset of projects is covered, and there is too little transparency about which ones are chosen and how to ensure compliance. Enforcement of the landmark Deforestation Regulation, meant to bar soy, cattle, timber and other commodities from the EU market unless proven to have no connection to deforestation, has now been pushed back twice under pressure from industry and trade partners. It is now set to enter force in December. As trafficking networks fan out across Europe, drug-related violence has shot up in and around port cities. Arguably, however, European states’ main concern is the cocaine pouring into their cities from South America, including via the Amazon trafficking route. As trafficking networks fan out across Europe, drug-related violence has shot up in and around port cities like Antwerp and Rotterdam, as well as in other hotspots in Italy, Spain, France and Germany. Crisis Group’s conversations with European officials suggest that curbing drug trafficking is a pressing policy concern for many governments and voters. Europe’s efforts to address drug trafficking in Latin America have already touched on the Amazon route, mostly through the now completed COPOLAD program. In Peru, for example, the program funded the creation of an early warning system to flag environmental crimes and criminal threats to human rights defenders. EU cooperation initiatives such as EL PAcCTO 2.0 have also funded projects to boost cross-border law enforcement cooperation on illegal gold mining. In late 2025, EL PAcCTO, Interpol and the Dutch police environmental crime unit aided Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana and Suriname in the first transnational operation to this effect , known as the Guyana Shield, which resulted in 198 arrests and seizures of illicit goods. Germany, for its part, has long funded the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO), while other European countries take part in specific initiatives on security in the region. France, for example, has deployed a liaison officer to the international police cooperation centre in Manaus, Brazil, created following the ACTO’s 2023 Belém Declaration . The EU is also supporting efforts to enhance border management and multinational frontier cooperation as well as to counter human trafficking in Latin America through EUROFRONT , including Amazon-region borders between Colombia and Ecuador. To tackle the challenges facing the Amazon, the EU and its member states should: Help improve law enforcement cooperation and legal harmonisation. The EU and its member states should pair seizures of illicit commodities with asset recovery and money laundering investigations that target the European counterparts of local criminal syndicates. The EU should also step up support for multinational law enforcement and expand port and container security cooperation with Amazon exit points such as Barcarena and the Guianas, where interdiction is weakest and cocaine shipments are on the rise. The EU and its partners should also push for legal harmonisation – eg, of illicit trafficking definitions in various penal codes – within the ACTO and Andean Community. To this end, the EU should support a proposal spearheaded by Brazil to add environmental crimes to the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime. Strengthen legislation governing gold and critical minerals markets. Critical raw materials refined outside the EU and imported as finished components fall outside the EU’s regulatory frameworks on conflict minerals and deforestation, while unrefined rare earths and bauxite are not covered at all. To ensure that its imports are not linked to criminal activity, the EU, its member states and its partners should support efforts such as those led by Brazil’s Federal Police and Colombia’s geological service to build gold and/or critical mineral traceability systems. The EU should also support law enforcement efforts targeting secondary products used in illicit mining, such as mercury, fuel, cyanide, explosives and mining equipment. Design a holistic approach toward the Amazon. The withdrawal of U.S. development aid has left gaps in environmental support and programming for alternative livelihoods in communities across the Amazon. While Europe cannot completely fill those spaces, the EU should focus support on market access, education and climate adaptation, particularly in coca-growing and gold-mining regions. Global Gateway – the EU’s strategy for financing infrastructure and connectivity projects in partner countries – should channel private investment toward sustainable infrastructure that could help make legal activities such as small-scale farming and fishing more commercially feasible, reducing the incentives for local communities to participate in illicit activity. Simultaneously, to slow deforestation, the EU should double down on results-based strategies such as that of the TFFF, which offers direct benefits to states that succeed in conserving forested areas. Back Indigenous governance. The EU and its member states should encourage capitals across the region to work closely with Indigenous organisations in monitoring illegal activities in remote jungles, since they are well placed to spot criminal activity where state security institutions are weak or absent.
