Israel’s Elections: What’s at Stake? eschelhaas Thu, 10/15/2026 - 18:12 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A Palestinian farmer walks past election banners near the Palestinian-owned olive groves in the village of Rantes near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on October 6, 2026. ZAIN JAAFAR / AFP Q&A / Middle East & North Africa 15 October 2026 16 minutes Israel’s Elections: What’s at Stake? Israelis will soon head to the polls for the first time since the 7 October 2023 attacks and the seismic events that followed. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts look at what issues concern the voters and what change the balloting may bring. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Related Tags Israel/Palestine What is happening? On 27 October, Israelis will head to the polls at a particularly fraught moment in the country’s history. The vote is the first since the deadly Hamas assault of 7 October 2023, which killed 1,318 Israelis and precipitated seismic events in Israel-Palestine and across the Middle East – not least Israel’s destruction of Gaza and killing of at least 74,000 of its people. The repercussions of this turmoil for Israeli electoral politics now wait to be seen. With Israel still entangled in several conflicts – including in the Palestinian territories, in Lebanon, in Syria and with Iran – and at the centre of increasingly passionate domestic political debates around the world, Israelis, Palestinians and millions of others will be watching closely. About a dozen political parties are expected to cross the proportional threshold (3.25 per cent of the national vote) needed to enter the parliament, or Knesset, which has 120 seats. Two main blocs – of nearly equal weight, according to polls – are facing off against each other. One is an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud Party. The other camp is led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar (meaning “straight”, as in honest), a centre-right party he founded in 2025. A third group, made up of parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian Arab minority, is projected to capture a smaller but critical share of seats. Defining party platforms is an inexact science. The vertical axis reflects domestic issues; the horizontal, external ones (including occupied territories). Box size reflects poll projections of seat numbers. Sources: israel-polls-2026.pages.dev. Party positions are Crisis Group assessments, building on Peter Lintl’s framework for Israel’s 2022 election, “Israel’s Anti-liberal Coalition”, Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik, 27 January 2023 / CRISIS GROUP Notwithstanding nuances among the various parties, the 2026 contest is largely a battle between different right-wing approaches to governing an Israel that has all but consolidated its control of the Palestinian territories – ie, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem. Questions that outsiders might expect to be at the centre of election debates, such as Israel’s almost 70-year occupation of these lands, preoccupy Israeli voters far less than internal issues, including the rule of law and relations between religion and state. That divergence raises complex questions about what change the world can expect to see after 27 October – and what is likely to stay the same. What are the chances of Netanyahu remaining in power? Significant, but it is too close to call. On one hand, the election comes at an especially tough time for Netanyahu. Poll numbers measuring his personal popularity and the degree of public trust he enjoys have been low for most of the period since 7 October 2023. His many years of domineering leadership – and in the view of former coalition partners, his corruption, manipulations and betrayals – have shrunk his pool of potential political allies. His Likud Party, the dominant force on the Israeli right since the 1970s, now polls lower than Eisenkot’s Yashar. Polls also show that given a choice between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, Israelis tend to favour the former general (who also garnered public sympathy after his son was killed in action in Gaza), over the sitting prime minister. For months, the parties that make up Netanyahu’s current coalition have together consistently polled well below the numbers needed for a 61-seat majority. A new hard-right party, Amcha Yisrael, led by former general Ofer Winter, could also be a handicap for Likud: it could draw votes away from Netanyahu’s party, but it could also “burn” votes, meaning render them irrelevant, since votes for smaller parties are discounted from the tally if they fail to cross the 3.25 per cent threshold. Yet Netanyahu, who turns 77 on 21 October, has long defied presumptions that his career has run its course. His skill at juggling crises is legendary; the latest ones include a lengthy trial for alleged corruption , widespread anger at his gradual overhaul of the judiciary, charges of failing to heed warnings ahead of the 2023 Hamas attack and then shirking responsibility for it, Israel’s sinking international reputation and an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, not to mention an open-ended, seven-front war spanning the Middle East. Some of his opponents, recalling what he has done in past election campaigns, worry that the pugnacious prime minister may resort to tactics aimed at dividing his opponents. In particular, they fear he may try to discourage or intimidate would-be voters among Israel’s Palestinian Arab citizens. Some are also apprehensive that, should he become desperate, Netanyahu might launch a new military action, perhaps against Iran, in an attempt to postpone the election . Regardless of any such manoeuvres, the far-right, religious, pro-settler coalition led by the prime minister is strong. It has survived four turbulent years in power and still enjoys a firm base of support, including among young and first-time voters. True, the Netanyahu bloc has consistently polled well below a majority needed to form a coalition, and the anti-Netanyahu bloc – a disparate collection of right-wing, centrist and centre-left Jewish parties, as well as two lists of Palestinian Arab parties – represents a bigger proportion of the electorate in raw numbers. But several of the latter camp’s Jewish leaders have publicly sworn they would not form a government with the Arab parties, implying they might even be loath to rely on these parties’ Knesset votes to bolster a minority coalition. With neither bloc able to reach a majority alone, the Arab parties look like kingmakers. But they will not join a Netanyahu-led coalition, and the anti-Netanyahu bloc is wary of inviting them into government. Source: Crisis Group estimates based on aggregate polling data up to 14 October. Some votes may be “lost” to parties that fail to reach the 3.25 per cent threshold. / CRISIS GROUP This reluctance to share power with Arabs is not new, but it has become a matter of political consensus since 7 October 2023. The Netanyahu camp’s repeated claim that its adversaries can only win by joining ranks with Arab parties is also a sign of how the far right now shapes the political climate: it appeals to anti-Arab prejudice to alarm voters and taunt opponents, as well as to trap them into possibly self-defeating commitments. The delegitimisation of any coalition that might include Arabs has increased Netanyahu’s chances of remaining as caretaker prime minister until another round of elections a few months later, not by winning, but by blocking the other side. What are the most important – and divisive – issues for Israeli voters? The elections are in part a referendum on Netanyahu, particularly on his responsibility (or lack thereof) for the 7 October 2023 events and his actions thereafter. Many Israelis blame him for a policy of accommodating Hamas’s rule in Gaza in the years leading up to the lethal attack, including the facilitation of Qatari financing; for reportedly ignoring warnings of an impending Hamas operation; for allegedly relegating Israeli hostages to the back burner among war priorities in Gaza; and for refusing to name an independent commission of inquiry into the intelligence and other failures that helped make the Hamas assault so deadly. Netanyahu’s supporters dismiss such charges as a political inquisition led by Israel’s “deep state” (which they allege includes judges and generals) along with left-leaning media and foreign-funded organisations. They defend the prime minister’s wars, arguing that he has smashed Hamas in Gaza and Hizbollah in Lebanon and (having persuaded the U.S. to join in) severely weakened the Islamic Republic of Iran, securing Israel’s uncontested regional primacy. The legacy of Netanyahu’s coalition, widely viewed as the most extreme in Israel’s history, is also at stake in that referendum. Since taking office in December 2022, the right-wing Likud and its harder-right partners have pursued an aggressive agenda of redesigning parts of the Israeli state, the occupation of the Palestinian territories and Israel’s regional surroundings. They have sought to weaken the judicial system as an institutional check (indeed the only remaining one) on the executive and legislature, at the same time as working to entrench government influence over Israeli media, tighten restrictions on civil society, extend religious laws and practices into various spheres of public life, and accelerate Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank. Meanwhile, they also stand accused of failing to support Jewish border towns affected by years of war, such as those near the Lebanese frontier, whose residents fled Hizbollah rocket fire and still consider it unsafe to return. Many Israelis who regard themselves as secular, socially liberal and advocates of mamlakhtiyut (meaning the primacy of the state over factional interests) view the government’s ambitions for extending its power as anathema. These critics accuse firebrand leaders such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir of endangering Israel’s democracy, its social cohesion and its image abroad. A fresh government unbeholden to the far right, they say, could help repair some of that damage. A dispute that encapsulates these multiple fissures concerns the conscription of Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) citizens into the Israeli army. Even as the Haredims’ share of Israel’s population grew from under 5 per cent in 1980 to nearly 15 per cent today, they continued to enjoy exemption from state service on religious grounds until 2024, when the Supreme Court overruled the exception. Two Haredi parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, which were formally part of Netanyahu’s coalition until mid-2025, sought to circumvent the ruling via new legislation that the prime minister promised to push. But they failed to reach an agreement that would pass the Knesset, as some members of the ruling coalition – including within Likud – favour universal conscription. In practice, most Haredi youths continue to dodge the draft. Opposition leaders ... dismiss partnering with Haredi parties unless they agree that their constituents should submit to the draft. The Haredim are deeply unpopular with many political factions. Opposition leaders, many of whom are secular or of military background, dismiss partnering with Haredi parties unless they agree that their constituents should submit to the draft. Pressure to enforce the law has mounted from exhausted army reservists whose lives have been disrupted by repeated call-ups over the last three years. The military has also repeatedly warned that it faces a personnel shortage, especially in light of the government’s demand that soldiers protect increasing numbers of settler outposts in the West Bank. For the 20 per cent of Israel’s citizenry who are Palestinian, the top issues are different. Many see blocking the far right as vital to protecting their precarious civil rights and to ensuring greater access to state resources, as well as to mitigating Israel’s worsening policies in the occupied territories. But most Arab voters also have a particularly urgent concern: restoring their personal safety amid an alarming surge in organised crime and gun violence in Arab towns, which has reached record levels under the watch of Ben-Gvir’s national security ministry and the police it oversees. The two Arab-led slates, the Joint List (made up of Hadash, which identifies as an Arab-Jewish socialist party; Ta’al, which describes itself as an Arab movement for renewal; and Balad, a Palestinian Arab nationalist party) and the Islamist Ra’am, in theory have the potential to become “kingmakers”. Neither the pro- nor anti-Netanyahu blocs will be able to reach a parliamentary majority without Arab support, either as part of a governing coalition or as outside votes to back a given coalition. But it is unclear how and to what extent such electoral clout can translate into collective gains when even most of Israel’s mainstream opposition reject partnering with them. The Arab parties themselves are not in lockstep; while Ra’am is seeking to join a coalition with only domestic concerns in mind, the Joint List stipulated that at least some demands relating to the occupied territories, such as a diplomatic pathway to a Palestinian state, must also be addressed in order for it to provide a “safety net” (ie, serve as external support) for a minority government. Is the conflict with the Palestinians playing a role in the elections? For the ruling parties, yes; for the opposition, barely. In addition to its war on Gaza, the Netanyahu government has spent its tenure hastening Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank and extending “Jewish sovereignty” through settlements, making the prevention of a Palestinian state its flagship goal. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a portfolio in the defence ministry, in particular has spearheaded efforts to advance de jure annexation. The Likud is promoting the slogan “Yamin o’ Falastin” (Hebrew for “ The Right or Palestine ”) to suggest that any alternative government would pave the way for Palestinian statehood, notably because it would depend on support from the Arab parties. Leading coalition figures loudly applaud the devastation of Gaza, with some others still promoting the expulsion of its people and the re-establishment of Jewish settlements in the strip. Opposition Jewish figures are less coherent or vocal on the topic, but by and large they do not call the settlement enterprise’s continuation into question. Some blast the government’s support for the more extremist settler agendas; virtually none supports Palestinian statehood, at least not in the near future; and many try to ignore the Palestinian question altogether. One possible exception is Avigdor Lieberman, a former defence minister and leader of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu, a party that largely represents Russian immigrants, and who proposes that Jordan assume responsibility for ruling Palestinians inside a truncated portion of the territory. The centre-left Democrats, led by reserve major general and parliamentarian Yair Golan, is perhaps the only Jewish party that openly supports a two-state solution, yet it conditions a Palestinian state on a host of caveats (such as maintaining long-term Israeli security control of the entire territory) and argues that in any case the time is not right for such a state to emerge. Only the two Arab lists consistently promote Palestinian rights and self-determination, though Ra’am largely relegates these issues to secondary importance in its campaign. One West Bank issue that has generated Israeli debate is mounting settler violence against Palestinians. One West Bank issue that has generated Israeli debate is mounting settler violence against Palestinians, with even Netanyahu condemning what he insists are “fringe groups”. What appears to concern Israel’s mainstream media and Jewish voters, however, is less the harm being done to Palestinians than the added burden being placed on Israel’s occupying army and the state’s resources. Many also lament the further blemishes on Israel’s international image. Next to nothing has been done to stop the attacks in practice, and official policies that more broadly immiserate West Bank Palestinians, such as economic strangulation , home demolitions and land expropriation, rarely elicit comment from the (non-Arab) opposition. In a late August interview, Eisenkot said the army had “lost its control” of the West Bank due to the Netanyahu government’s policies and its emboldening of settler vigilantes. He also criticised the push to build the controversial E1 settlement , which would split the West Bank in two, as a “mistake” that has angered Israel’s allies. In a more recent interview , he claimed that a Yashar-led government would not only curb the actions of what he has called “Jewish terrorists” but also evacuate all outposts considered illegal under Israeli law in the West Bank (under international law, all settlements on occupied territory are considered illegal). It is fair to assume that he might also freeze construction of E1. But Eisenkot has also described the two-state solution as “delusional” and stressed that “I very much believe in settlement in Judea and Samaria” (the biblical term that many Israelis use for the West Bank). Naftali Bennett – head of the Together slate, a former prime minister and past head of the Yesha settler council – is unapologetic about his support for annexing the West Bank’s Area C (ie, the part that the 1993-1995 Oslo accords left under full Israeli administrative and security control) and his rejection of Palestinian statehood. The same is true of opposition figure Lieberman, as well as two other prominent politicians, Benny Gantz and Yoaz Hendel, who have positioned themselves as unaligned with either bloc. The competing parties may differ over whether to prop up the Palestinian Authority with financial and security cooperation and who should govern Gaza, but these are peripheral rather than central disagreements. Vis-á-vis the Palestinians, the next Israeli government will assume power on a markedly different footing from when the current one was elected four years ago. In the interval, Israel has swallowed more territory and squeezed Palestinians into smaller cantons in both Gaza and the West Bank. It has razed cities and refugee camps and emboldened a settler movement that will likely remain feverishly active regardless of who is in power. There is now near-consensus among Israeli Jews about maintaining security control throughout the occupied territories – from the proverbial river to the sea. But while the far right wants to turbo-charge the settlement enterprise and turn up the heat on the Palestinians further, many Israelis would prefer to bracket the issue, reverting to policies that can manage the conflict on their terms rather than seeking a political agreement with the Palestinians. The latter approach kept the occupation out of sight and out of mind – but also kept its end out of reach. Such shades of difference could change the level of physical and economic violence meted out to Palestinians, which is no small matter. But they would barely touch the core of the occupation itself. Have Israel’s other military campaigns in the region – in Lebanon, Syria and Iran – influenced the domestic political scene? Surprisingly little. A majority of Jewish Israelis has consistently supported Israel’s wars, with tens of thousands of soldiers and reservists continuing to serve despite widespread disillusionment with Netanyahu’s government. Even when Israelis were forced into shelters for weeks on end during the present war with Iran, public support remained high. In many ways, the seven-front war of the past three years has simply accelerated Israel’s rightward shift. Such criticism as there is tends to demand a harder, not softer approach. The centrist opposition leader Yair Lapid, whose Yesh Atid party is running alongside Bennett on the Together slate, said Israel should not have stopped at assassinating Iran’s leadership but should have bombed its oil and gas facilities during the second phase of the war, which started in late February. Bennett, for his part, has made classifying Qatar as an enemy state a central talking point. In November 2024, days before a ceasefire was brokered between Lebanon and Israel, Gantz, an ostensibly centre-right former general, called on the military to bomb Lebanese government assets. What are the most likely outcomes? Barring a dramatic development, and assuming the most credible polls are largely correct, four plausible scenarios could emerge after election day: A hung parliament. Neither bloc wins a decisive parliamentary majority or ropes enough parties into supporting a minority government. This outcome is possible, for instance, if Eisenkot or his allies refuse to bring the Arab lists into the fold or to rely on their outside support. The result would be another round of elections. In this case, Netanyahu would stay on as caretaker prime minister, with his sitting coalition continuing to hold the reins of government for several months, pending a fresh vote. Yashar edges out Likud and forms a government drawn from the opposition. This scenario would likely require Eisenkot to partner in some fashion with the two lists that represent Palestinian citizens – perhaps as external backers, instead of coalition partners – with the principal aim of keeping Netanyahu and his bloc out of power. There is precedent for this arrangement (albeit in starkly different circumstances), such as when Arab parties gave outside support to Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin from 1992 until his assassination in 1995. But shifts in public opinion, especially after the 7 October 2023 attacks, make reliance on the Joint List in particular a politically fraught proposition. Parties or politicians break ranks. Following an inconclusive result, Eisenkot or Netanyahu could convince parties or individual Knesset members in the opposing bloc to defect and form a “national unity government”. There could be several permutations along these lines. For example, commentators have suggested that the opposition consider forming a government with Likud, excluding far-right parties such as Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit. Netanyahu himself has floated this possibility. Though it got broadly negative responses, there is recent precedent, albeit with mixed results. In 2020, Netanyahu persuaded Gantz, then his biggest rival, to join a coalition, causing Gantz’s Blue and White Party to split. The government dissolved only a few months later. A bloc defies the polls and clinches a parliamentary majority. This outcome is highly unlikely. It would mean that months of polls have been egregiously wrong, given that all have said neither bloc is close to winning 61 seats. A surprise could conceivably occur if several parties fail to cross the electoral threshold, thus “burning” a large share of votes, or if turnout for certain parties far exceeds expectations. Israel’s electoral system has always been prone to twists and turns, but the 2026 election’s result is arguably less predictable than usual. Dry numbers from various sources provide hints. An independent aggregator of opinion polls over recent months suggests that the chances of either bloc achieving an outright majority are well under 10 per cent. Online betting sites , which are a rough indicator of where investors put their money, give Eisenkot and Yashar slightly greater respective odds of becoming the next prime minister and largest party in the Knesset. Still, even in that scenario Eisenkot would have to decide whether to partner with Arab parties, a question he has skirted until now. The outcome may not be all that stable. Despite a reshuffling of parties and emergence of new personalities, and though the political spectrum as a whole has shifted further rightward, Israeli voters appear to be caught in the same deadlock that has largely held since 2019 – one that led Israeli voters to go to the voting booths five times in three years until the current government took office – and held onto it for four years. The recent uptick in international pressure on Israel’s West Bank policies – notably, the UK-led settlement trade ban in September – is unlikely to fundamentally shift Israeli views in the near term, though it may affect voter turnout for one side or the other. Many Israelis are distrustful or dismissive of foreign criticism, believing that outsiders do not understand their nation’s unique circumstances, are overly fixated on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or harbour anti-Israeli or anti-Semitic views. That said, they are not oblivious to the threat of isolation. They know that Israel’s brutal Gaza war, its increasingly aggressive policies in the West Bank and the proliferation of Middle East conflicts have all come at a high reputational cost to Israel, not only harming its diplomatic standing but also affecting its citizens’ interactions with the outside world. The question is whether mounting outside pressure can constructively shift Israeli calculations on war and peace after election day – regardless of the coalition that emerges. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/16/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 16 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 16 October 2026 IRAN Iranian attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in October to date, with more than two dozen vessels struck since the month began. Meanwhile, Washington is maintaining its blockade of Iranian ports while backing oil shipments along the Omani coast, where smaller tankers transfer cargo to larger vessels outside the strait. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick in Iranian strikes is an effort to counter a rebound in oil flows that showed Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was weakening. Iran wants Washington to accept its proposed terms for a ceasefire that reopens the waterway in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. blockade. But a diplomatic breakthrough appears less likely than the two sides setting off another escalatory spiral. SUDAN The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a UN-backed hunger monitor, warned Monday of growing famine risks in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, driven by conflict, displacement and inadequate aid funding, and compounded by an El Niño-induced drought. This news comes as Sudan’s army reports advances against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in parts of North Kordofan and West Darfur. Meanwhile, the RSF continues to mount attacks in Blue Nile and to target El Obeid in North Kordofan with drones. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says the army’s gains could make it more confident of victory, while continued RSF offensives suggest that this group, too, sees opportunities for battlefield gains. The continued fighting is likely to further complicate diplomatic efforts to end the war and ease Sudan’s humanitarian crisis. UKRAINE This past Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, saying each had agreed to halt attacks on the other’s energy infrastructure, following a deal he made to buy Russian diesel and ease related U.S. sanctions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he learned of the ceasefire through social media, adding that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries. Ukrainian forces also reported restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, which they depend on for communications and drone operations. Washington says it continues to share intelligence with Ukraine. Zelenskyy this week announced the resumption of refinery attacks as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued unabated. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says any disruption to intelligence or communications would compound Ukraine’s difficulties in protecting its cities and power grid as winter approaches, leaving civilians more vulnerable to prolonged heating and electricity outages. 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. IRAN - U.S. The fragile April ceasefire between Washington and Tehran wobbled as the two sides engaged in increasingly sharp exchanges of fire. U.S. forces launched repeated strikes on Iranian targets as Tehran retaliated by targeting U.S. bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait; Iran and Israel also traded blows for the first time in two months. On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened that the U.S. would take control of Kharg island, site of Iran’s main oil terminals, and other energy infrastructure. He backtracked later in the day, cancelling new strikes and insisting that a negotiated deal with Tehran was close. WESTERN SAHARA A Moroccan airstrike on Sunday killed three Polisario Front members who were carrying out an attack on Moroccan fortifications in Western Sahara. Among the dead was Lehbib Mohamed Abdelaziz, son of Polisario’s former secretary general, who had been rumoured to be a candidate to become the Front’s leader. Cepeda promises to reduce inequality and continue talks with armed groups, while de la Espriella advocates iron-fist policies, including bombing organised crime groups, building mega-jails and restoring traditional values. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says Petro’s claims raise concerns over a peaceful transfer of power if Cepeda loses, while Trump’s involvement has fuelled resentment over foreign interference, which could further trigger demonstrations. CONFLICT-RELATED SEXUAL VIOLENCE The UN on 29 May released its annual report on conflict-related sexual violence, showing that reported cases more than doubled in 2025 after rising 25 per cent the year before. UN Women also recently reported that in Sudan alone, the number of women and girls needing support after sexual violence has quadrupled since civil war broke out three years ago. Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing says survivor services are increasingly scarce after major U.S. aid cuts in 2025 hit programming for which Washington had been the largest donor. Compounding the problem, Washington’s February 2026 “Protecting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance” policy restricts aid recipients’ work and speech on abortion. Though the policy’s ban on “promoting” abortion exempts cases of rape, many NGOs fear inconsistent enforcement and unclear compliance requirements, leaving them to choose between U.S. conditions that may limit post-rape care and refusing funding at the risk of jeopardising their wider operations. LEBANON Israel and Lebanon on Wednesday agreed to a new U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal, which would establish pilot zones in southern Lebanon where Hizbollah operatives would be barred. Crisis Group expert Max Rodenbeck says the Board’s strategy of making relief for Gaza’s people, whether humanitarian aid or broader hopes for the future, conditional on Hamas’s willingness to surrender its arms is deeply troubling and a recipe for prolonging their misery. KOREAN PENINSULA Pyongyang said it tested two new missiles Tuesday, including a short-range, nuclear-capable cruise missile that it plans to deploy with troops facing South Korean soldiers across the Korean peninsula’s demilitarised zone. Along with Pyongyang’s growing closeness to Moscow and questions about Washington’s commitment to defending South Korea amid its mounting competition with Beijing, the tests are likely to bolster the consensus in Seoul behind more intensive military modernisation of its own. MALI As many as 50 people were killed Wednesday in jihadist raids on two villages in the central Mopti region, underscoring the breadth of the threat posed by the al-Qaeda affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM). Already, nearly 5.9 million refugees have come back since September 2023, many of them forced to do so by harsh Pakistani visa policies amid rising tensions between Islamabad and the Taliban authorities in Kabul. Now the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will likely compel many Afghans living in the Islamic Republic to leave, even as the exodus from Pakistan continues. Many of these people are women, who will face draconian Taliban restrictions on freedom of movement and economic activity. The returnees also include children, some of whom have never even been to Afghanistan and will be at greater risk of child marriage, which the Taliban have lately recognised as a legal act. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says international donors should give generously to fund the $529 million UN response plan, without which many returnees will be destitute. NIGERIA The military announced Tuesday that joint strikes carried out with the U.S. had killed 175 jihadist fighters in the preceding week, in addition to destroying stockpiles of arms. The strikes began on 16 May with one that killed Abu Bakr al-Mainuki, deputy leader of the Islamic State-West Africa Province (ISWAP), who had been coordinating activities with jihadists in the Sahelian countries. At a hearing in Washington on Tuesday, General Dagvin Anderson, head of U.S. Africa Command, told U.S. legislators that “the epicentre of global terrorism is in Africa”. They are a setback for ISWAP, at least for the time being. U.S. - CUBA The U.S. indicted former Cuban leader Raúl Castro Wednesday for murder and conspiring to kill U.S. nationals. The charges relate to a 1996 incident in which Cuban fighter jets shot at planes flown by anti-Castro Cuban Americans trying to help Cubans escape the island. These legal developments arrive amid renewed speculation that the Trump administration intends to decapitate the Cuban regime much as it did the Venezuelan government with its raid to snatch former President Nicolás Maduro in early January. Senior U.S. officials, most recently Central Intelligence Agency head John Ratcliffe, have held a series of semi-secret meetings with high-ranking figures in Havana this spring. Publicly, Cuban leader Miguel Díaz-Canel has remained defiant, rejecting the allegations against Castro as a “political manoeuvre”. Meanwhile, the U.S. has tightened a blockade of Cuba that has precipitated a humanitarian crisis and sent additional warships to the Caribbean Sea. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says any attempt to forcibly break the tight grip the Cuban Communist Party and military have upon the state could result in violent chaos and further suffering for the Cuban people. 15 May 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO A spate of lethal violence in the north-eastern Ituri province over the past two weeks has underscored the complexity of the country’s crisis. In late April, a group of Codeco militiamen killed at least 69 people, mainly civilians, in a series of separate attacks. Allied with the Congolese government, Codeco claims to defend the interests of the Lendu people, most of whom are farmers, from encroachment by ethnic Hema herders. According to local sources, it raided several Hema villages in retaliation for assaults on Congolese army positions by a Hema armed group. The province has been under martial law since 2021, the same year that Uganda (with Kinshasa’s permission) sent in troops to pursue ADF militants based in Congolese territory. War and violence drove some 32.3 million people from their homes in 2025, the most ever, representing a 60 per cent increase over 2024. The internal displacements in Iran and the Democratic Republic of Congo made up two thirds of the global total. Crisis Group President and CEO Comfort Ero says these numbers are a sobering reminder of how pervasive conflict has become in today’s world. The human cost of war is never abstract. U.S. - CHINA U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping concluded their long-awaited summit Friday. Nor did it bring a major reversal, which some in Taiwan had feared, such as Trump agreeing to scale back U.S. arms sales or change Washington’s longstanding declaratory policies toward the island. The summit was nonetheless illuminating in two respects. First, it underscored Trump’s desire to gain a greater foothold in China for U.S. businesses as well as his conviction that a strong working rapport with Xi can produce a cooperative relationship between Washington and Beijing. ETHIOPIA A showdown may be looming in Tigray, Ethiopia’s northernmost region, after its ruling party reinstated a state council Tuesday that was dissolved immediately before the bloody 2020-2022 Tigray war. U.S. - CHINA Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due to host U.S. President Donald Trump in Beijing next week for a long-awaited summit, which had been slated for the end of March. In exchange, Xi may try to extract security concessions from Trump, perhaps by asking him to lessen U.S. defence backing for Taiwan or to declare that the U.S. “opposes“ (rather than “does not support“, which is the longstanding U.S. position) Taiwanese independence. 1 May 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Fresh violence between Afghanistan and Pakistan erupted this week. Pakistan denied targeting civilians, saying its strikes aimed at militants, based on intelligence. COLOMBIA Nearly two dozen people are dead and scores injured after a series of apparently coordinated attacks in the country’s south west that authorities blamed on Estado Mayor Central (EMC), a dissident faction of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia. Militants used drones, explosives and roadblocks to hit targets including police stations and military bases. On 25 April, improvised explosive devices went off on a major highway in Cauca, striking a bus and other civilian vehicles, killing at least twenty. ROHINGYA Nearly 900 Rohingya refugees died or were reported missing while trying to make perilous sea crossings in 2025, the UN said last week. The new Bangladeshi government should permit Rohingya to secure jobs in sectors with labour shortages. The more ways the Rohingya have to earn a living in refuge, the fewer of them will risk their lives at sea. IRAN Amid a widening Middle East conflict sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes that began two weeks ago, the Islamic Republic effected only the second transition in its most senior post since the 1979 revolution that brought it to power. Mojtaba Khamenei has taken up the position of Supreme Leader, which his father Ali held from 1989 until his death on 28 February in the war’s opening salvo. The U.S.-Israeli campaign has continued unabated, doing significant damage. Iran has responded with drone and missile strikes in the Gulf and brought traffic in the Strait of Hormuz to a crawl. The first official statement attributed to the younger Khamenei was defiant in tone, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, highlighting the Iranian regime's desire to project continuity under duress, vis-à-vis both its foreign adversaries and its domestic opponents. But that ambition could be short-lived if Khamenei is targeted amid the hostilities or outmanoeuvred by other players in the regime's upper echelons. Many Iranians, meanwhile, are despairing at a leadership transition that so far promises more of the same. LEBANON Israel’s latest military escalation in Lebanon continued to wreak havoc this week. Since 2 March, when Hizbollah fired rockets toward Israeli territory for the first time in over a year, Israel has ramped up aerial bombardment, including of the capital Beirut, and forced hundreds of thousands to flee their homes. It has also sent more troops into southern Lebanon, with a view to establishing what it calls a “security zone” there. While Israel retains military superiority over Hizbollah, the Shiite party-cum-militia has put up a fight. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Already, the Lebanese public has paid a horrific price: the death toll has climbed to almost 700, and thousands more have seen their homes and communities destroyed. 6 March 2026 IRAN The U.S. and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran Saturday, hitting military installations and killing senior leaders, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. The U.S.-Israeli campaign appears open-ended, with no clear objective yet defined. Airstrikes can substantially degrade Iran's military capabilities but are unlikely to dislodge the regime, and even if they did, state collapse in Iran would risk unleashing far wider regional disorder. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. The declaration followed Taliban retaliatory cross-border attacks after Pakistani airstrikes on purported Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) targets in Afghanistan on 21 February. Pakistan then carried out another series of strikes on 27 February, including in Kabul. Islamabad accuses Taliban authorities of sheltering the TTP, which has stepped up attacks in Pakistan. Kabul denies it. According to the UN, the latest fighting has killed dozens of civilians in Afghanistan and displaced tens of thousands, with reports also indicating civilian casualties in Pakistan. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Cuba is facing considerable uncertainty after U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday urged its government to “make a deal” or face the consequences, vowing that the U.S. would cut the Venezuelan oil supply to the island nation, which is heavily dependent on these deliveries for its energy needs. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case.
